Narrative: Spiny mice (Acomys) are the only mammals known to regenerate full-thickness skin — including hair follicles, sebaceous glands, and arrector pili muscles — without scarring. When threatened by a predator, they shed large patches of skin (autotomy) and regrow it completely, something no lab mouse can do. The regeneration extends beyond skin: Acomys can regenerate ear hole punches (including cartilage), kidney tissue after ischemia-reperfusion injury, and spinal cord tissue after injury — all with minimal fibrosis compared to Mus musculus. Gusev's group at Kazan Federal University (Filatov 2024) revealed a distinctive hemostasis phenotype: spiny mouse blood forms stronger hemostatic seals with elevated clottable fibrinogen, denser fibrin-rich clots, and superior plasma clot stiffness. This robust hemostasis may be an adaptation that enables the risky strategy of shedding skin — you need reliable clotting before you can afford to lose tissue. The molecular drivers are still being mapped: Acomys wounds show reduced TGF-beta signaling, a macrophage response biased toward pro-regenerative rather than pro-fibrotic polarization, and Wnt pathway activity resembling embryonic patterning rather than adult scarring. No single gene has been identified as the master switch — this appears to be a systems-level rewiring of the wound response. The challenge for translational work is moving from descriptive -omics to causal gene targets.
Short Description: Skin punched clean through heals back whole—hair follicles, glands, and cartilage regrow instead of scarring, driven by low TGF-beta signaling and clot-forming blood 2-3x stronger than a lab mouse's. A 4mm ear hole closes in about 60 days with full structure restored, versus permanent scarring in Mus. This exists only in the Cairo spiny mouse—no transgenic transfer into mice attempted. No master gene runs it: TGF-beta, macrophage signaling, and Wnt patterning would need rewiring together.
Mechanism: Systems-level wound response: reduced TGF-beta/fibrotic signaling; pro-regenerative (M2-like) macrophage polarization; Wnt pathway activity resembling embryonic patterning; distinctive hemostasis with elevated fibrinogen and denser fibrin-rich clots (Filatov 2024). Regeneration includes hair follicles, sebaceous glands, cartilage, and potentially kidney and spinal cord tissue.
Achievements (effect sizes): Seifert 2012 Nature: Acomys regenerated 4mm ear punches with cartilage, hair follicles, and sebaceous glands in ~60 days (Mus scarred). Brant 2015: full-thickness dorsal skin wounds healed without fibrosis. Filatov 2024 IJMS: Acomys blood formed 2-3× stronger fibrin clots vs Balb/c mice. Simkin 2017: kidney ischemia-reperfusion — Acomys showed reduced fibrosis and preserved nephron architecture. Matias Santos 2023: ear regeneration involves blastema-like structure with Wnt/beta-catenin signaling.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (multiple mammalian organ systems) + T6 (replicated across independent labs)
Translational Gaps: No single master-switch gene identified; systems-level program likely requires multiple coordinated interventions; no transgenic experiments transferring Acomys wound program to Mus; no human-cell studies; hemostasis-regeneration link is correlative, not causally demonstrated.
Key References (DOIs): Seifert Nature 2012 https://doi.org/10.1038/nature11499 | Filatov IJMS 2024 https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms252312867 | Brant Wound Repair Regen 2015 https://doi.org/10.1111/wrr.12319 | Simkin Nat Commun 2017 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-017-01671-5
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: NOT a single-gene candidate — included as a systems-level enhancement program. Translating Acomys regeneration may require rewiring TGF-beta signaling, macrophage polarization, and Wnt patterning simultaneously. Hemostasis connection (Filatov 2024) is from Gusev's lab but causal relationship between clotting phenotype and regeneration is unproven. Acomys are small rodents; whether the program scales to larger mammals is unknown. Some regenerative capacity (ear punch) may be shared with other Acomys species that differ in autotomy ability, suggesting the programs are separable.

Manipulation: overexpression (root-specific promoter in a heterologous plant host)
Narrative:
Chinese brake fern, Pteris vittata, grows on mine tailings and does something no flowering plant can do: it draws arsenic out of the soil and stockpiles it in its fronds at more than one percent of its dry weight (https://doi.org/10.1105/tpc.109.069773). That is a load that would be lethal in almost any other tissue. The trick is a transporter. Arsenate entering the root is reduced to arsenite on the way up, and PvACR3 — an arsenite efflux permease sitting in the membrane of the vacuole rather than in the cell surface — pushes that arsenite out of the cytosol and into the vacuole, where it is simply stored. The cell never detoxifies the metalloid. It puts it in a box and shuts the lid.

The evolutionary detail is what makes the gene worth exhibiting. ACR3 is present in mosses, lycophytes, other ferns and gymnosperms, and it has been lost in every angiosperm — which includes every crop we eat. Flowering plants threw the machinery away. Putting it back is therefore not the enhancement of an existing capability but the restoration of a discarded one, and in 2025 a group did exactly that: rice transformed with PvACR3 under a rice root-specific promoter became an arsenic pump, hauling the metalloid out of flooded paddy soil and into its own shoots (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eehl.2025.100168).

That result is a gift for soil cleanup and a disaster for dinner. The transgenic rice inverts the wild-type distribution of arsenic in the plant: wild type keeps most of its arsenic below ground, while the transgenic lines have significantly less in the root and hundreds of milligrams per kilogram in the shoot. For remediation that is the whole point, because the arsenic can be walked off the field in a wheelbarrow. For food it is fatal, because the shoots have to be harvested and disposed of as hazardous biomass before grain filling. Nobody has put this gene into an animal, and the first obstacle is anatomical rather than technical: animal cells have no vacuole to put anything into.
Short Description: A membrane pump moves arsenic out of the cytoplasm and locks it inside the vacuole, so a body can carry a dose of arsenic that would otherwise kill it — over one percent of its dry weight — without being poisoned. Rice given the fern's transporter under a root-specific promoter piled 452-557 mg/kg of arsenic into its shoots, 19 to 24 times more than wild type, and stripped 23.5 times more arsenic out of the same contaminated paddy soil. The fern itself is already planted in the field for arsenic phytoremediation; the transgenic rice exists only in hydroponics and pots, and no animal has ever been given the gene. The catch is that the transporter relocates arsenic upward rather than destroying it, so the shoots must be cut and hauled away as hazardous biomass before the grain fills and the plant can never be eaten. In an animal the same logic holds: the arsenic is still inside you, held in a compartment, and it leaves only when that compartment does.
Mechanism: Arsenate entering the root is reduced to arsenite before or during its journey to the frond. PvACR3 is a roughly 379-amino-acid, 41.6 kDa permease with ten predicted transmembrane helices, a member of the ACR3/ArsB family of arsenite efflux carriers. Its location is the point. In yeast the equivalent protein sits in the plasma membrane and throws arsenite out of the cell, whereas PvACR3 localises to the vacuolar membrane and instead moves arsenite from the cytosol into the vacuole, where the fern keeps it as free arsenite rather than as a glutathione or phytochelatin complex. Pteris vittata carries a duplicated pair of these genes, ACR3 and ACR3;1, and only ACR3 is arsenic-inducible in the tissues that contact soil. The family occurs in mosses, lycophytes, other ferns and gymnosperms but has been lost from every angiosperm lineage, which is the structural reason no flowering plant hyperaccumulates arsenic without help.
Achievements (effect sizes): Characterisation of the transporter in its native fern established both the phenotype and the causal link. “Gametophytes of the fern Pteris vittata can accumulate and tolerate more than 1% of their dry weight as arsenic”, and RNA interference against ACR3 — but not against its duplicate ACR3;1 — made those gametophytes arsenite-sensitive, while PvACR3 rescued the arsenic-sensitive phenotype of a yeast strain lacking its own ACR3 (Indriolo 2010, https://doi.org/10.1105/tpc.109.069773). Transferred into rice under the root-specific promoter pLsi1, the same gene turned a staple crop into an arsenic pump: in hydroponic culture “pLsi1::PvACR3 lines exhibited 37.1-50.3-fold and 19.2-23.7-fold higher shoot As concentrations than WT under 5 uM (268-364 mg/kg) and 20 uM (452-557 mg/kg) treatments, respectively (p < 0.05)”, against wild-type shoot concentrations of only 7.24 and 23.5 mg/kg (Zhu 2025, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eehl.2025.100168). The same lines were then grown in flooded pots of moderately arsenic-contaminated paddy soil, where the transgenic rice “removed 23.5 times more As from the same paddy soils” than wild-type rice, reaching 45.9-80.3 mg/kg arsenic in the shoot and almost completely depleting arsenic from the soil pore water when the shoots were harvested before grain filling (Zhu 2025, https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eehl.2025.100168).
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (native loss-of-function in the source fern plus heterologous gain-of-function in a crop, demonstrated in both hydroponics and contaminated soil, by multiple laboratories)
Translational Gaps: No animal has ever received this gene, and the reason is anatomical before it is technical. Mammals handle arsenic by a different route entirely: arsenite methyltransferase (AS3MT) methylates arsenite, and the methylated products leave the body in bile and urine, so mammalian detoxification is chemical modification followed by export rather than storage. Animal cells also have no vacuole, so a mammalian version of this card would have to retarget the transporter to the lysosome, and nobody has attempted that experiment. There is no experimental structure either: the fold of ACR3-family permeases is known only from homology modelling and AlphaFold prediction, so the ten-helix architecture described here is a prediction rather than a measurement. Even within plants the evidence stops at hydroponics and pot trials, and the question of what happens to arsenic-loaded biomass after harvest has not been answered experimentally.
Key References (DOIs): Indriolo The Plant Cell 2010 https://doi.org/10.1105/tpc.109.069773 | Zhu Eco-Environment & Health 2025 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eehl.2025.100168 | Ma Nature 2001 https://doi.org/10.1038/35054664
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The discovery paper for the hyperaccumulation phenotype is Ma 2001 in Nature (https://doi.org/10.1038/35054664). Its DOI resolves, but the full text could not be retrieved while this record was prepared, so no number in this entry is taken from it and it is listed as a reference only. The commercial picture is unusual for this library: Pteris vittata itself is already planted deliberately for arsenic phytoremediation, so the wild-type version of this enhancement is in field use, while the transgenic rice exists only in laboratory hydroponics and pot experiments (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.eehl.2025.100168). Field deployment has documented limits — Wan and colleagues report that soil texture and climate constrain where fern-based phytoremediation actually works (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jhazmat.2022.129151). The transporter was isolated and characterised in the Banks laboratory at Purdue University, which also localised it to the vacuolar membrane and showed the gene is absent from all angiosperms (https://doi.org/10.1105/tpc.109.069773). The reference sequence is UniProt E3URE9 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/E3URE9); there is no Protein Data Bank entry, so any structural image is a model. There are no clinical trials, and it is worth saying plainly why that is appropriate: this gene concentrates a carcinogenic metalloid rather than eliminating it.

Narrative: Arctic fish don't freeze because they're full of proteins that grab microscopic ice crystals the moment they form and glue themselves onto the crystal faces, stopping growth. The translational question is whether these molecules can do the same for mammalian tissue. The answer, so far, is a qualified yes. Adding 20 mg/mL of Type III antifreeze protein to standard mouse-ovary vitrification media raised intact follicle recovery from 28.9% to 44.7% — a big effect for cryobiology, where incremental gains are normal. AFPs have been used in clinical IVF oocyte freezing for years. Korkut Uygun's team at Harvard pushed the concept further, supercooling human donor livers to −4°C with AFPs and extending viable ex-vivo time by about 27 hours. The next step — actually transplanting a supercooled human liver — is imminent, not hypothetical. Chronic-exposure immunogenicity remains unresolved, and more AFP isn't always better: at high doses you can cause ice-needle damage.
Short Description: This protein grabs ice crystals the instant they form and clamps onto their faces, blocking growth so tissue survives freezing. In mouse ovary vitrification, 20 mg/mL raised intact follicle survival from 28.9% to 44.7%. It's already used in clinical IVF oocyte freezing, and a Harvard team supercooled a human liver to -4°C, adding about 27 hours of viable storage before transplant. Push the dose too high, though, and the protein forms damaging ice needles.
Mechanism: Non-colligative freezing-point depression via ice-face binding; thermal hysteresis; ice-recrystallization inhibition; membrane/ion-channel stabilization.
Achievements (effect sizes): Transgenic salmon (Hew 1991–99): stable Mendelian inheritance, seasonal AFP in serum but levels insufficient for seawater freeze-avoidance. Tobacco Type-I AFP (Kenward 1993): protein accumulated; Type-II AFP gave NO frost resistance despite 2% apoplast protein. Drosophila+beetle AFPs enhanced cold survival. Bagis 2006/2008: Type-III AFP-Tg mice, F7 germline; cryopreserved ovaries/testes retained function; live offspring after orthotopic ovary transplant. 20 mg/mL AFP in mouse ovary vitrification media: 44.7% intact follicle ratio vs 28.9% control (Lee 2015, PLoS ONE). Amir/Rubinsky 2004: AFPs in −1.3 °C 21-h rat heart preservation. AFPs in IVF oocyte vitrification (clinical-grade). Toner/Uygun/Tessier: supercooled human livers to −4 °C extended ex-vivo viability ~3× (+27 h); 2022–2024 partial-freezing 10-day rat liver storage at −10 to −15 °C.
Highest Evidence Tier: T6 (human ex-vivo organs, IVF cells) + T5 (Tg mice with functional tissue cryopreservation)
Translational Gaps: Supercooled human livers not yet transplanted; immunogenicity under chronic exposure.
Key References (DOIs): Bagis Mol Reprod Dev 2006 https://doi.org/10.1002/mrd.20601 | Lee PLoS ONE 2015 (AFP ovary cryo) https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0126252 | de Vries Nat Biotechnol 2019 (supercooled liver) https://doi.org/10.1038/s41587-019-0223-y
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Dose-response non-monotonic (ice-needle damage at higher concentration); Tg frost tolerance inconsistent. Kenward 1999 tobacco Type-II — no frost protection despite high expression. AquaBounty salmon uses growth hormone not AFP for phenotype.

Manipulation: overexpression (level-tuning; the enzyme sets the red/yellow balance)
Narrative:
Parrots come in red and yellow versions of the same bird with unnerving regularity: the dusky lory has a red morph and a yellow morph, lovebirds put red on the face and green on the back, and breeders have been shuffling these colours for generations without knowing what they were shuffling. The answer turns out to be almost embarrassingly simple chemistry. Parrot pigments, the psittacofulvins, are linear conjugated polyene chains, and whether one looks red or yellow depends on what sits at the end of the chain. An aldehyde end group gives red. Oxidise that aldehyde to a carboxylic acid and the same chain gives yellow.

The enzyme that performs the oxidation is not a specialist. ALDH3A2 is the fatty-aldehyde dehydrogenase of ordinary lipid metabolism, present in essentially every cell of the follicle and in every tissue of a vertebrate body, and the parrot has simply recruited it as a colour control. Mapping two species independently pointed at the same locus: in rosy-faced lovebirds the enzyme's transcript tracked the green-versus-red patches within a single bird, and in dusky lories a genome scan across both morphs converged on a variant sitting just past the end of the gene (Arbore 2024, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adp7710). Yeast supplied the causal test. Running an avian polyketide synthase in a strain with the yeast counterpart of ALDH3A2 deleted, then restored, shifted the end-group chemistry of the pigments exactly as predicted.

What makes this a genuinely different enhancement from making the pigment in the first place is that it is a dial rather than a switch. Because the phenotype comes from how much enzyme is present, not from which enzyme, the carboxyl-to-aldehyde ratio and therefore the hue is continuous, and it is set locally, patch by patch, in late-differentiating keratinocytes. The unavoidable cost is that the dial is wired to something else. Turning a housekeeping lipid enzyme up or down for cosmetic reasons changes fatty-aldehyde clearance in every tissue that expresses it, and human genetics is unambiguous about what happens when this particular enzyme fails.
Short Description: A single enzyme dial sets whether a patch of your skin comes out red or yellow: turn it up and red goes to yellow, turn it down and the same patch runs red. It works by oxidising the aldehyde end group of a polyene pigment to a carboxylic acid, and within one lovebird the green patches carried 4-6-fold more of the enzyme's transcript than the red patch on the same head. The whole story comes from parrot genetics and a yeast reconstitution, with the causal change being a non-coding variant 42 base pairs downstream of the gene rather than anything in the protein. That regulatory location is what makes it hard to copy: you cannot buy the phenotype by expressing a cDNA. The cost is that this is not a pigment enzyme by trade but the ubiquitous fatty-aldehyde dehydrogenase of lipid metabolism, and losing it in humans causes Sjogren-Larsson syndrome, with scaly skin, spastic diplegia and intellectual disability.
Mechanism: Parrot plumage colour is set by which chemical form of psittacofulvin is deposited: red psittacofulvins carry an aldehyde end group and yellow ones a carboxyl group. ALDH3A2, aldehyde dehydrogenase 3 family member A2, also known as fatty-aldehyde dehydrogenase (FALDH) and normally responsible for oxidising medium- and long-chain fatty aldehydes, oxidises the aldehyde end group of psittacofulvins to the corresponding carboxylic acid. Because what varies between red and yellow birds is the expression level of the enzyme rather than its protein sequence, the enzyme functions as a continuous dial on the carboxyl-to-aldehyde ratio, and therefore on hue, in late-differentiating keratinocytes of the feather follicle. Yeast reconstitution confirmed the step directly: an avian polyketide synthase construct expressed in a strain with HFD1, the yeast ortholog of ALDH3A2, either knocked out or restored produced the corresponding shift in psittacofulvin end-group chemistry.
Achievements (effect sizes): Three independent lines of quantification converge on the same enzyme. Bulk RNA sequencing of regenerating feather follicles from eight rosy-faced lovebirds, sampled at three green patches on back, chest and head plus one red patch on the head, found 4-6-fold higher expression in the three green feather patches compared to the red, and chemical analysis of the same feathers showed the green patches carrying a higher carboxyl-to-aldehyde psittacofulvin ratio, which is the direction the mechanism predicts (Arbore 2024, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adp7710). Independently, whole-genome resequencing of 57 dusky lories spanning both colour morphs (red n = 35, yellow n = 22, at mean depth 11.5 +/- 4.8x) identified three associated variants inside a 284 bp interval, of which one SNP (scaffold_13:6,288,712T>C) showed a markedly stronger association with color ( P = 6 x 10 -14 ), sitting in non-coding sequence 42 bp downstream of the longest ALDH3A2 transcript (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adp7710). Allele-specific expression closed the loop within individual birds: bulk RNA sequencing plus full-length long-read transcriptomes of regenerating follicles from red (n = 3) and yellow (n = 3) lories showed the two alleles transcribed unequally at 71% yellow vs. 29% red , chi 2 , P = 0.03 (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adp7710). Single-cell and single-nucleus chromatin-accessibility profiling localised the activity to the follicle, and the yeast knockout and knock-in experiments demonstrated the enzymatic conversion itself.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (association mapping in two parrot species, allele-specific expression, single-cell and snATAC-seq localisation, plus yeast knockout/knock-in reconstitution of the enzymatic step)
Translational Gaps: The yeast experiments demonstrate the chemical conversion only qualitatively. Products were identified by ultra-high-performance liquid chromatography with high-resolution accurate-mass quadrupole time-of-flight mass spectrometry, but the study reports no conversion percentage and no kinetic constants, so the efficiency of the step is unmeasured. The causal variant is regulatory and non-coding, lying 42 base pairs downstream of the transcript, which means that reproducing the phenotype requires reconstructing a cis-regulatory context in the right cell type rather than simply delivering a complementary DNA. The association is also not absolute: the lead variant matched phenotype in 98% of individuals rather than in all of them, and five individuals were discordant at the two flanking variants, so at least one additional modifier is unaccounted for. Nothing has been attempted in a mammal, and any mammalian attempt inherits the problem that the enhancement requires psittacofulvins to be present in the first place, which no mammal makes.
Key References (DOIs): Arbore Science 2024 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adp7710
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: This card is deliberately paired with the budgerigar polyketide synthase entry as the downstream hue-control step acting on the same pigment chemistry, but it is a separate gene doing separate chemistry: aldehyde oxidation of a finished chain rather than synthesis of the chain (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.adp7710). No parrot ALDH3A2 UniProt accession could be retrieved. UniProt returns avian ALDH3A2 entries for chicken, quail and kakapo (Strigops habroptila, A0A672UIG9, https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A0A672UIG9) among others, but none for Agapornis roseicollis or for the dusky lory, so the kakapo protein is the nearest psittacine reference sequence and should be labelled as a cross-species substitute rather than as the lovebird enzyme. A methodological detail worth knowing before anyone tries to repeat the yeast work: the strain background was Saccharomyces cerevisiae BJ5464-NpgA, and the polyketide synthase used was the chicken enzyme (LOC420486) rather than the budgerigar one, because it gave higher polyketide yields. There is a direction trap in the clinical literature. ALDH3A2 appears there only as the Sjogren-Larsson syndrome disease gene, where loss of function causes ichthyosis, spastic diplegia and intellectual disability, which is the opposite framing from this card's gain-of-expression enhancement; no trial administers or upregulates the enzyme, and none tests the colour phenotype.

Manipulation: base editing knockout (adenine base editor delivered by GalNAc-lipid nanoparticle to hepatocytes); also natural loss-of-function
Narrative: ANGPTL3 was found the way several of the best lipid targets were found: by noticing people who were unusually healthy. Sequencing across the DiscovEHR cohort turned up 246 heterozygotes among European-ancestry participants, roughly 1 in 237, whose blood carried about half the normal amount of the protein and correspondingly less fat - and who reached the clinic with coronary artery disease considerably less often than everyone else (Dewey 2017, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1612790). The protein is a hepatokine, made by the liver and released into blood, where it does nothing more complicated than sit on two enzymes and stop them working: lipoprotein lipase and endothelial lipase, the machines that strip triglycerides out of circulating lipoproteins. Remove the brake and both lipases run faster. What lifted this from an interesting genotype to a clinical program is a property that sounds technical and is actually decisive: the LDL-lowering half of the effect does not need the LDL receptor. For a patient with homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, whose LDL receptors do not work at all, statins and PCSK9 inhibitors have little to push against - the entire mechanism they rely on is missing. ANGPTL3 loss bypasses it. Getting an editor into such a liver posed its own version of the same problem, because the standard lipid nanoparticle also arrives via the LDL receptor. The fix was to decorate the particle with GalNAc sugar so it docks instead on the asialoglycoprotein receptor, and it worked spectacularly in LDL-receptor-deficient monkeys (Kasiewicz 2023, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-37465-1). Two companies are now doing this in living patients. Both trials are single-ascending-dose, both are primarily asking whether it is safe, and both write a change into the genome that no one yet knows how to undo.
Short Description: Switching off a liver-secreted brake on fat clearance releases two lipases at once, so triglycerides and LDL cholesterol fall together after a single infusion instead of a daily pill. In monkeys bred without a working LDL receptor, one dose of a GalNAc-targeted base editor raised liver editing from 5% to 61% and held circulating ANGPTL3 protein down by up to 89% at six months. Two Phase 1 trials are recruiting patients right now - VERVE-201 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06451770) and CTX310 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07491172) - and the same pathway is already drugged by the approved antibody evinacumab. Humans born with one inactive copy carry 27% lower triglycerides and 41% lower odds of coronary artery disease, though the heart-attack arm never reached significance. The edit is a permanent letter change in hepatocyte DNA: monkeys showed transient rises in the liver enzymes ALT and AST, and there is no way to dial it back if a carrier later needs their lipids.
Mechanism: ANGPTL3, angiopoietin-like protein 3, is a 460-amino-acid hepatokine: the liver makes it and secretes it into the bloodstream, where it inhibits two enzymes that hydrolyse circulating fat, lipoprotein lipase and endothelial lipase. Losing the protein de-represses both, so triglyceride-rich lipoproteins are broken down faster and their remnants cleared sooner. The LDL-cholesterol-lowering arm of the effect does not require the LDL receptor, and that independence is the whole clinical rationale, because it makes the mechanism usable in homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia where the LDL-receptor route is simply absent. The therapeutic version installs the loss permanently instead of inhibiting the protein repeatedly. An adenine base editor - a Cas9 protein fused to a deaminase, supplied as messenger RNA together with a guide RNA - is packaged inside a lipid nanoparticle whose surface carries an N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) ligand. That ligand binds the asialoglycoprotein receptor on hepatocytes, giving the particle a way into liver cells that does not depend on the LDL receptor. Once inside, the editor converts a single adenine to guanine at a splice or coding position, disrupting the gene without cutting both DNA strands, so one infusion produces a knockout that persists as the cell divides rather than a drug level that has to be maintained.
Achievements (effect sizes): Humans born with one inactive copy of the gene have "27% lower triglyceride levels than noncarriers (P = 2.5x10-21), 9% lower LDL cholesterol levels (P = 2.8x10-5), and 4% lower HDL cholesterol levels (P = 0.02)", and "a 41% lower odds of coronary artery disease (adjusted odds ratio for any loss-of-function variant, 0.59; 95% confidence interval [CI], 0.41 to 0.85; P = 0.004)" across up to 45,226 DiscovEHR participants (Dewey 2017, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1612790). The same study puts carrier frequency at 1 in 237 participants of European ancestry and confirms haploinsufficiency biochemically, with median protein of 50 ng/mL in 125 carriers against 99 ng/mL in 53 matched noncarriers (P = 9.4x10-16); the myocardial-infarction arm, however, was only numerically lower (odds ratio 0.66, 95% CI 0.39 to 1.06, P = 0.09) and should not be cited as a significant benefit. On the therapeutic side, adding a GalNAc ligand to the lipid nanoparticle "increased liver editing from 5% to 61% with minimal editing in nontargeted tissues" in LDL-receptor-deficient monkeys, produced "durable blood ANGPTL3 protein reduction up to 89% six months post dosing" against 13% for a standard particle, and drove blood LDL cholesterol down by 35% - roughly a 100 mg/dL absolute fall - stable for three months (Kasiewicz 2023, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-37465-1). Specificity and dose-sensitivity were both quantified in the same work: across 17 additional sites and tissues, editing outside the liver stayed under 2%, while in Ldlr-knockout mice "as little as 0.01 mol % GalNAc-Lipid substantially rescued editing to a mean of 26.3%" from 1.3% with none at all, and 0.05 mol % gave the best result of 31.4%, with higher ligand densities performing worse.
Highest Evidence Tier: T9 (human clinical - two independent Phase 1 in vivo gene-editing trials actively recruiting, backed by human loss-of-function genetics n>58,000 and single-dose nonhuman-primate durability to 6 months)
Translational Gaps: Neither editing trial has released human efficacy data. VERVE-201's Phase 1b primary endpoint is safety - treatment-emergent and serious adverse events through Day 365 - and the numbers a visitor would care about, percent change in serum ANGPTL3, LDL cholesterol and triglycerides, are secondary endpoints only (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06451770). Durability in monkeys has been shown to six months and no further, so anyone claiming a lifelong knockout is extrapolating from half a year of primate data. The permanence works in both directions: because the editor rewrites hepatocyte DNA rather than occupying a protein, there is no dose to reduce and no way to restore the gene if a recipient later needs their lipid transport intact, for instance during a wasting illness or a pregnancy. Most importantly, no outcome trial exists for any ANGPTL3 editor, so the claim that editing prevents heart attacks rests entirely on carrier genetics - an odds ratio of 0.59 for coronary artery disease in people who were born this way (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1612790) - rather than on any edited human having avoided an event.
Key References (DOIs): Dewey New England Journal of Medicine 2017 https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1612790 | Kasiewicz Nature Communications 2023 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-37465-1 | Pinzon Grimaldos Journal of Translational Medicine 2025 https://doi.org/10.1186/s12967-025-07448-5
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: A direction audit matters here, because the registry is crowded with the opposite modality. Of 46 ClinicalTrials.gov records returned for ANGPTL3, only two are gene-editing interventions in which the gene itself is the treatment: VERVE-201 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06451770), base editing, and CTX310 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07491172), a Cas9 nuclease. The remainder are antisense and small interfering RNA agents (vupanorsen, zodasiran/ARO-ANG3, olezarsen-class, ALN-ANG3, solbinsiran), the approved antibody evinacumab (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT03452228), observational carrier studies such as the University of Pennsylvania physiology protocol (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04234724), and a long tail of records where the protein was merely measured as a biomarker, including pecan- and cottonseed-oil feeding studies and a ketogenic-diet trial. Two Novartis cartilage-regeneration trials of LNA043 also surface in these searches and have nothing to do with this gene. Verve's earlier VERVE-101 and VERVE-102 programs target PCSK9, not ANGPTL3, and should not be conflated with the separate pcsk9_edit entry in this library. On the biology of the low-lipid state itself, a 2025 study of familial combined hypolipidemia type 2 reports that lipid deprivation amplifies type I interferon responses in monocytes through altered protein prenylation, meaning the immune cells of a lipid-poor body behave measurably differently (Pinzon Grimaldos 2025, https://doi.org/10.1186/s12967-025-07448-5). Pharmacological inhibition of the same pathway is already approved: evinacumab (Evkeeza, Regeneron) is licensed for homozygous familial hypercholesterolaemia, a different modality reaching the same axis. Reference structures are UniProt Q9Y5C1 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q9Y5C1) and the single solved structure PDB 6EUA (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/6EUA).

Manipulation: Loss-of-function knockout (human null variants R19X / IVS2+1G>A / IVS3+1G>T)
Narrative:
Most cardiovascular genetics is about cholesterol. This one is about the other half of the lipid problem: the fat-laden particles that leave the gut and liver after a meal, and how fast the body takes them apart. Apolipoprotein C-III is a small protein that rides on those particles and acts as a brake, blocking the enzyme that hydrolyses their triglyceride in the capillary bed and slowing their removal by the liver. Some people are born without a working copy of it, and the brake is never installed.

In 2014 two research groups arrived at the same answer from opposite directions in the same issue of the same journal. One sequenced the exomes of thousands of Americans, found four rare loss-of-function variants in the gene, and tested them against coronary disease in 110,970 people. The other went through 75,725 participants of two Danish population studies with 10,797 incident vascular events on the books. Carriers had triglycerides 39% and 44% lower respectively, and their risk of coronary heart disease was 40% lower in the American cohort and 41% lower for ischemic vascular disease in the Danish one. That kind of agreement between an exome-sequencing study and a population cohort is unusually strong replication for a rare-variant result.

What makes this card different from most of the library is that the enhancement is already for sale, and the FDA has read the file. Ionis Pharmaceuticals built an antisense oligonucleotide that finds the messenger RNA for this protein inside hepatocytes and destroys it — a pharmacological imitation of being born a carrier — and sells it as TRYNGOLZA for familial chylomicronemia syndrome and severe hypertriglyceridemia. Arrowhead reached the same target by RNA interference with plozasiran. A visitor buying this gene is buying a phenotype that roughly one person in 150 already has, that two independent cohorts of a hundred thousand people agree about, and that two companies have independently turned into a product.
Short Description: Deletes the brake on fat clearance, so triglyceride-rich particles are stripped out of the bloodstream within hours instead of lingering — the inhibitor that normally shuts down lipoprotein lipase in the capillary bed is simply absent. Roughly one person in 150 already carries such a broken copy, and they run 39% lower triglycerides for life with 40% less coronary heart disease (odds ratio 0.60). The pharmacological version is on sale: olezarsen, marketed as TRYNGOLZA, is an FDA-approved antisense drug that silences the same protein in the liver and cut triglycerides by 53.1 percentage points against placebo at its higher dose. The catch is that this is not the LDL axis — in the same trial olezarsen lowered apolipoprotein B and non-HDL cholesterol but produced no significant change in LDL cholesterol, so LDL-driven atherosclerosis is left untouched. The germline allele is free and permanent; the drug is a monthly injection for life.
Mechanism: Apolipoprotein C-III (apoC-III) is a 99-amino-acid protein secreted by liver and intestine that coats chylomicrons and very-low-density lipoprotein (VLDL). It works as a double brake on the clearance of triglyceride-rich lipoproteins: it inhibits lipoprotein lipase (LPL), the enzyme that hydrolyses triglyceride as those particles pass through the capillary bed, and it inhibits hepatic uptake of the leftover remnant particles through the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR) and LDL receptor-related protein 1 (LRP1). Nonsense and splice-site null alleles remove the inhibitor altogether, so LPL runs unopposed and remnants are cleared faster. Because that clearance route is driven by LPL and remnant receptors rather than by the LDL receptor pathway, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol is essentially unchanged — the cardiovascular protection arrives entirely through the triglyceride-rich lipoprotein axis. The antisense and RNA-interference drugs reproduce the same state by destroying the messenger RNA in hepatocytes rather than by altering the gene.
Achievements (effect sizes): Exome sequencing of 18,666 genes in 3,734 participants identified rare loss-of-function variants in APOC3, and follow-up association testing in 110,970 people compared 498 carriers against 110,472 noncarriers. Triglyceride levels in carriers were 39% lower than in noncarriers (P<1×10^-20), circulating apoC-III was 46% lower (P=8×10^-10), and coronary heart disease risk was 40% lower, with an odds ratio of 0.60 (95% CI 0.47–0.75; P=4×10^-6); about one person in 150 carried one of the four variants (Crosby / TG-HDL Working Group 2014, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1307095). Independently, 75,725 participants of the Copenhagen City Heart Study and Copenhagen General Population Study, contributing 10,797 incident ischemic vascular disease events, showed a mean reduction in nonfasting triglycerides of 44% (P<0.001) in heterozygotes, a 41% lower risk of ischemic vascular disease (hazard ratio 0.59; 95% CI 0.41–0.86; P=0.007) and a 36% lower risk of ischemic heart disease (HR 0.64; 95% CI 0.41–0.99; P=0.04) (Jørgensen 2014, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1308027). The pharmacological phenocopy has since been tested head-to-head against placebo: in Bridge-TIMI 73a, a phase 2b randomized trial in 154 patients at 24 North American sites with a median baseline triglyceride of 241.5 mg/dL, olezarsen reduced triglycerides by 49.3 percentage points at 50 mg and 53.1 percentage points at 80 mg relative to placebo over six months (P<0.001 for both) (Bergmark 2024, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2402309).
Highest Evidence Tier: T8 (human loss-of-function genetics in more than 180,000 people, replicated across two independent cohorts, plus an FDA-approved drug that phenocopies the allele)
Translational Gaps: The 40% reduction in coronary heart disease is a property of the germline allele, measured in people who were born without the protein and lived their whole lives that way. The drugs deliver a comparable triglyceride reduction over months rather than decades, and cardiovascular outcome trials for apoC-III lowering have not yet reported, so nobody has yet shown that starting the knockdown in middle age buys the same protection from heart attacks. Full biallelic APOC3 deficiency in humans is very rare and its long-term phenotype is essentially uncharacterised, which means the exhibit's version of this gene — both copies gone — is less well described in humans than the single-copy version the epidemiology rests on. The approved indications are also narrower than the enhancement framing: the label covers familial chylomicronemia syndrome and severe hypertriglyceridemia, not primary prevention in healthy people.
Key References (DOIs): The TG and HDL Working Group of the Exom New England Journal of Medicine 2014 https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1307095 | Jørgensen New England Journal of Medicine 2014 https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1308027 | Bergmark New England Journal of Medicine 2024 https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa2402309
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The two 2014 papers reached the same conclusion by different routes — United States exome sequencing (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1307095) versus Danish population cohorts (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1308027) — which is unusually strong replication for a rare-variant association. Two companies now sell an apoC-III-lowering agent by different modalities: olezarsen is a GalNAc-conjugated antisense oligonucleotide approved as TRYNGOLZA under NDA 218614 (Ionis), given as a monthly subcutaneous injection at 80 mg for familial chylomicronemia syndrome and 50 mg for severe hypertriglyceridemia, and plozasiran is a quarterly small interfering RNA marketed by Arrowhead as REDEMPLO. The pivotal records are the Balance phase 3 study (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT04568434) and PALISADE (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05089084), with further phase 3 recruitment ongoing (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07727538). Where the literature disagrees is on which agent is better: matching-adjusted indirect comparisons find no statistically significant efficacy difference between olezarsen and either volanesorsen or plozasiran in familial chylomicronemia syndrome (https://doi.org/10.57264/cer-2026-0069 and https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jacl.2026.05.001), so claims of superiority between these drugs are not currently supported.

Narrative: One woman in Colombia should have lost her mind by her forties. She carried PSEN1-E280A, a mutation that guarantees early-onset Alzheimer's in the world's largest autosomal dominant kindred — over 6,000 family members around Medellín. Instead, she remained cognitively intact until her seventies, three decades past the expected onset. The reason, reported by Arboleda-Velasquez in Nature Medicine in 2019, was two copies of an extraordinarily rare APOE variant called Christchurch (R136S). Her brain was loaded with amyloid but had remarkably little tau pathology and neurodegeneration. In 2018, Huang's group at Gladstone had already shown that converting APOE4 to APOE3 by CRISPR in human iPSC-derived neurons rescued tau phosphorylation, amyloid-beta overproduction, and GABAergic neuron loss. In 2023, Nelson and Huang engineered the R136S mutation into APOE4 mice and iPSC neurons and found that homozygous Christchurch edit rescued APOE4-driven tau pathology, neurodegeneration, and neuroinflammation. The idea of editing a patient's APOE4 alleles to a protective form is now the sharpest genetic target in Alzheimer's prevention. The catch: nobody has delivered a brain-wide APOE edit in a living animal, and APOE2 homozygosity itself raises cardiovascular lipid risk.
Short Description: This liver-made protein clears amyloid junk from between brain cells; the risky version slows cleanup, letting plaque pile up. A Colombian woman with a guaranteed early-onset mutation carried two rescue copies and stayed sharp into her seventies, thirty years past schedule. CRISPR-editing the risky version reverses tau damage in human neurons and mice, but nobody has edited a living brain. Two rescue copies also give 5-10% of people artery-clogging lipid disorder.
Mechanism: APOE: 299-aa secreted glycoprotein; E4 (Arg112/Arg158), E3 (Cys112/Arg158), E2 (Cys112/Cys158); Christchurch = R136S. E4 promotes Aβ aggregation, impairs Aβ clearance via LRP1/HSPG, increases tau phosphorylation. E2/Christchurch reduce HSPG binding, preserve microglial lipid homeostasis, diminish neuroinflammation.
Achievements (effect sizes): Wang 2018 Nat Med: iPSC APOE4/4 neurons showed increased p-tau, increased Aβ42/40, GABAergic neuron loss; CRISPR E4→E3 RESCUED all phenotypes. Nelson 2023 Nat Neurosci: APOE4-R136S homozygous in PS19 tauopathy mice rescued tau pathology, ~40% hippocampal volume loss prevented, neuroinflammation reduced. Arboleda-Velasquez 2019 Nat Med: PSEN1 carrier homozygous for APOE3-Christchurch — clinical onset delayed ~30 years.
Highest Evidence Tier: T6
Translational Gaps: No in-vivo brain-wide APOE editing in any animal; AAV/LNP BBB delivery; off-target base editing; APOE2/2 dysbetalipoproteinaemia risk (~5–10% of E2 homozygotes); mosaicism concerns.
Key References (DOIs): Wang Nat Med 2018 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-018-0004-z | Arboleda-Velasquez Nat Med 2019 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41591-019-0611-3 | Nelson Nat Neurosci 2023 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41593-023-01480-8
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: APOE2 HOMOZYGOSITY carries its own risk: ~5–10% develop type III hyperlipoproteinaemia. Christchurch mutation is extraordinarily rare — single-case evidence. The Colombian woman had APOE3 background, not APOE4; whether R136S rescues E4 in humans is inferred from mice only. APOE4 effects are species-specific: E4 increased Aβ in human but NOT mouse neurons. Heterozygous R136S only partially protective.

Narrative: Aquaporins are tiny membrane pores that let water flow through cells about ten times faster than simple diffusion. Peter Agre won the 2003 Nobel for discovering them, after putting human AQP1 into frog eggs and watching them swell and burst. In mammals, knocking out AQP1 leaves mice producing dilute urine and losing weight when water is scarce — though the human version of this defect (Colton-null blood group) is essentially symptomless. The Australian water-holding frog survives months of drought in a cocoon, and is often cited as having a super-charged AQP1, but here's the awkward truth: the frog's actual AQP1 has never been cloned or tested in the lab. The entire chain — identify the special frog gene, transfer it to mammals, enhance hydration — is missing its first link. Even worse for the premise: in lungfish, AQP1 mRNA goes down during estivation, not up.
Short Description: Water channels made of this protein punch tiny pores in membranes, letting water cross about ten times faster than plain diffusion. Mice missing it lose 35% of body mass under water deprivation, yet Colton-null humans with the same defect feel nothing. The drought-surviving frog credited with a supercharged version has never had its actual AQP1 cloned or tested in any lab. In lungfish, the closer real data point, AQP1 activity drops during dry-season dormancy instead of rising.
Mechanism: Constitutively active water-selective tetrameric channel; ubiquitous in mammals.
Achievements (effect sizes): AQP1 generally: Preston 1992 (Agre) Xenopus-oocyte Pf 10–20× rise. Ma/Verkman 1998: AQP1-KO mice have 5–8× reduced proximal tubule Pf, 35% body-mass loss on water deprivation; urine osmolality 1081→505 mOsm. Colton-null humans subclinical. Cyclorana-SPECIFIC AQP1 has NOT been cloned or functionally characterized — source-organism work is whole-animal (bladder storage up to 50–60% body mass; plasma 487 mOsm/kg during 15-month estivation; Cartledge 2008). Desiccation tolerance is cocoon + metabolic depression + AQP2-type skin channels + urea, not AQP1 alone.
Highest Evidence Tier: T7 for mammalian endogenous AQP1 (Colton-null); T0–T1 for Cyclorana-specific AQP1
Translational Gaps: Entire frog-AQP-enhancement chain is missing: Cyclorana AQP cDNA not published; no heterologous expression in mammalian systems.
Key References (DOIs): Preston Science 1992 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.256.5055.385 | Ma JBC 1998 https://doi.org/10.1074/jbc.273.8.4296 | Cartledge Physiol Biochem Zool 2008 https://doi.org/10.1086/588489
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: CONTRADICTION to more-AQP1=more-retention model: lungfish aqp1 mRNA DECREASES during aestivation induction (Chng 2016) — opposite direction. Colton-null humans are asymptomatic → gain-of-function unlikely to be dramatic. Mammalian AQP1 phenotype is mild at baseline.

Narrative: Bats carry deadly viruses (Ebola, SARS-CoV-2, Nipah) without getting sick — a superpower rooted in their unique immune system. Bat ASC2 is a PYD-only protein that potently suppresses inflammasome assembly, preventing the runaway inflammation that kills other mammals during viral infection. Four key amino acid substitutions make bat ASC2 dramatically more effective than its human counterpart, representing an evolutionary solution to the inflammation-longevity tradeoff.
Short Description: Bats hold their inflammatory alarm below the level where it damages their own tissue, which is why flight and constant virus exposure do not cook them from the inside. Four bat-specific amino acids make their version about ten times better at this than the human one. Transgenic mice carrying it survived influenza A better and shrugged off gout crystals and SARS-CoV-2 inflammation. Paratus Sciences raised $100M on it, though capping inflammation is also how you get immunosuppressed.
Mechanism: ASC2 competitively binds NLRP3 and AIM2 inflammasome PYD domains, blocking ASC speck formation and preventing caspase-1 activation and IL-1beta/IL-18 release. Four bat-specific residues (compared to human ASC2) confer ~10x stronger inhibition, effectively capping the inflammatory response below tissue-damaging thresholds.
Achievements (effect sizes): Transgenic mice expressing bat ASC2 showed reduced gout-crystal peritonitis, dampened multi-virus inflammation, reduced influenza A mortality, and suppressed SARS-CoV-2 inflammasome activation. Paratus Sciences launched with $100M to develop ASC2-inspired therapeutics.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5
Translational Gaps: Human ASC2 exists but is far weaker; gene therapy would need to deliver the bat-specific variant. Risk of immunosuppression. Paratus Sciences PS-1001 compound in preclinical development.
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: $100M commercial validation (Paratus Sciences). Strongest commercial interest among new genes.

Narrative: The Icelandic genetics company deCODE did something only Iceland makes easy: it whole-genome sequenced 2,636 people, imputed those genomes into a national cohort of roughly 398,000, and went looking for rare variants that moved cholesterol. What surfaced was a 12-base-pair deletion sitting in the fourth intron of ASGR1, the gene for the main subunit of the asialoglycoprotein receptor - a liver lectin known for half a century as the machine that pulls aged, desialylated glycoproteins out of the bloodstream, and known to nobody as a cholesterol gene. Carriers had less coronary artery disease, and they had it consistently: the association held in Iceland, Denmark, the Netherlands, the United States and New Zealand, with a heterogeneity P value of 0.96 (Nioi 2016, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1508419). A second, entirely separate truncating mutation in the same gene, p.W158X, reproduced the lipid effect in an independent sequenced set, which is about as close as human genetics gets to a replicated experiment. What makes this variant interesting as an enhancement rather than as a curiosity is that it works outside the axis every existing lipid drug occupies. Statins, PCSK9 inhibitors and LDL-receptor biology all converge on the same clearance route; ASGR1 loss does not. That is why the field has begun trying to install it on purpose in people whose LDL receptors do not work at all. There is a sharp irony buried in the enhancement, though. The receptor this gene encodes is the exact molecular handle that GalNAc-conjugated drugs and GalNAc-decorated lipid nanoparticles grab in order to reach the liver at all - the same handle the ANGPTL3 base editor elsewhere in this library depends on. An enhanced human who buys ASGR1 loss has quietly given up the front door to their own liver.
Short Description: Disabling one copy of a liver receptor that mops up worn-out, sugar-stripped proteins also lowers the cholesterol that clogs arteries, by a route that has nothing to do with statins. Icelanders born with the 12-base-pair del12 deletion, about 1 in 120 of them, carry non-HDL cholesterol 15.3 mg/dL lower than their neighbours and have 34% less coronary artery disease, a result that replicated across eight populations with no heterogeneity at all. No drug or editor aimed at this target has entered a clinical trial, although a 2026 report describes deliberately installing the same loss by liver base editing. The cost is a permanent biochemical fingerprint: carriers run alkaline phosphatase about 46.5 U/L high, which in any ordinary clinic triggers a workup for cholestatic liver disease they do not have. The same receptor is the docking site that GalNAc-tagged liver drugs use to get into hepatocytes, so losing it may put an entire class of liver therapies out of reach.
Mechanism: ASGR1 encodes the major subunit of the asialoglycoprotein receptor, also called the Ashwell-Morell receptor, a calcium-dependent C-type lectin displayed on the surface of hepatocytes. Its normal job is surveillance of circulating glycoproteins: when a protein loses the terminal sialic acid caps from its sugar chains, exposing galactose and N-acetylgalactosamine, the receptor binds it and pulls it into the cell for degradation. The del12 allele is a 12-base-pair deletion inside intron 4 that activates a cryptic splice site; the resulting transcript is frameshifted and carries a premature stop codon, and the truncated protein is prone to degradation, so a person with one del12 copy is functionally haploinsufficient rather than merely carrying a mildly altered receptor. Losing half of that clearance capacity lowers non-HDL cholesterol by a route independent of the LDL receptor and PCSK9 axis; the leading explanation involves altered hepatic handling of glycosylated ligands and a consequent shift in cholesterol traffic, but the causal chain has not been closed. The pharmacodynamic fingerprint is unambiguous, because serum alkaline phosphatase is itself an asialoglycoprotein receptor ligand: when the receptor stops clearing it, it accumulates in blood, which is why every carrier can be spotted from a routine liver panel.
Achievements (effect sizes): Heterozygous carriers of the del12 deletion carry non-HDL cholesterol lower by "a difference of 15.3 mg per deciliter (0.40 mmol per liter) (P=1.0x10-16)" than noncarriers, measured across roughly 398,000 imputed Icelandic genomes, and their fasting triglycerides are lower by 6.3% (95% CI -10.3 to -2.3, P=0.003, n=99,893) (Nioi 2016, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1508419). The clinical consequence is a "lower risk of coronary artery disease (by 34%; 95% confidence interval, 21 to 45; P=4.0x10-6)", corresponding to a combined odds ratio of 0.66 (95% CI 0.55 to 0.79) that held across eight study populations in Iceland, Denmark, the Netherlands, the United States and New Zealand with no detectable heterogeneity (P=0.96), and to a hazard ratio of 0.64 for a first myocardial infarction among Icelandic carriers (P=8.5x10-5). The deletion is carried by 1 in 120 persons in that study population, and a second independent truncating allele, p.W158X, carried by 1 in 1850 persons, was also associated with lower non-HDL cholesterol (P=1.8x10-3) - an internal replication using a different mutation in the same gene. The same dataset quantifies the price: alkaline phosphatase is raised by a combined 46.5 U/L (95% CI 40.1 to 52.7, P=5.6x10-69, n=131,889) and vitamin B12 by 16.6 pmol/L in the Icelandic set (95% CI 11.5 to 21.5, P=3.1x10-12) (Nioi 2016, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1508419).
Highest Evidence Tier: T7 (human natural-experiment genetics; two independent loss-of-function alleles, n>390,000, replicated across 8 populations, no therapeutic yet)
Translational Gaps: No drug, antibody or genome editor directed at this target has entered a registered clinical trial, so every number in this record comes from people who were born with the variant rather than from anyone who was given it. The mechanism connecting a lectin that clears desialylated glycoproteins to a 15.3 mg/dL fall in non-HDL cholesterol has not been established: Nioi 2016 (https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1508419) demonstrates the association and the pharmacodynamic marker, not the causal pathway. Every human studied is heterozygous - no homozygous null humans are described anywhere in the cohort - so the complete knockout an exhibit visitor would actually be buying has never been observed in a person, and its phenotype cannot be predicted from the heterozygous data. The receptor also performs jobs the cohort does not track over a full lifespan, notably the clearance of desialylated platelets and von Willebrand factor, so consequences for coagulation over eighty years remain unmeasured. Finally, because this receptor is what GalNAc-conjugated drugs and GalNAc-lipid nanoparticles use to enter hepatocytes, someone lacking it may be refractory to an entire delivery platform, including the ANGPTL3 base editor in this same library.
Key References (DOIs): Nioi New England Journal of Medicine 2016 https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa1508419
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: This entry collides with another one in the library, and the collision is mechanical rather than thematic. The asialoglycoprotein receptor that ASGR1 builds is exactly the receptor that GalNAc-decorated lipid nanoparticles exploit to reach hepatocytes: Kasiewicz 2023 (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-023-37465-1) raised liver ANGPTL3 base editing from 5% to 61% in LDL-receptor-deficient monkeys precisely by adding a GalNAc-asialoglycoprotein-receptor ligand to the particle. Buying ASGR1 loss and ANGPTL3 base editing in the same body is therefore self-defeating, and an exhibit visitor who selects both has built a contradiction. Separately, the field has started running this variant forward rather than merely observing it: a 2026 Molecular Therapy paper reports hepatic base editing of ASGR1 as a deliberate LDL-receptor-independent lipid-lowering strategy (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ymthe.2026.07.036), retrieved here as metadata only and not read in full, so no figures from it are quoted. One transcription caution for anyone checking the source: the published confidence interval for the first-myocardial-infarction hazard ratio reads "0.64; 95% CI, 0.64 to 0.80", which does not bracket its own point estimate; it is reproduced in this record exactly as printed rather than silently corrected. The protein and structure references are the human entries UniProt P07306 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P07306) and PDB 1DV8 (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/1DV8), one of eight solved structures.

Manipulation: Three-factor transcription-factor reprogramming of cochlear supporting cells (inducible transgene / AAV)
Narrative:
In 1988 two laboratories reported the same impossible thing: a bird that had been deafened by loud sound grew its hearing organ back. Working in adult Japanese quail, Ryals and Rubel traumatised the basilar papilla, then watched dividing cells appear in an epithelium that textbooks said was finished at hatching, and counted hair cells climbing back to within 5 percent of the number the birds started with (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.3381101). Mammals cannot do this. The support cells that sit between our hair cells are the same cell type that, in a bird, would re-enter the cell cycle and become sensory; in us they scar over and the loss is permanent, which is why noise-induced and antibiotic-induced deafness is for life.

The obvious move was to hand mammalian support cells the master switch the birds use. ATOH1, a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor, is the gene that tells an inner-ear progenitor to become a hair cell, and in 2005 an adenovirus carrying Atoh1 was reported to improve hearing thresholds in deafened guinea pigs (https://doi.org/10.1038/nm1193). Novartis built a drug on that result — CGF166, an adenoviral vector delivering human ATOH1 injected into the labyrinth — and took it into 22 people with severe-to-profound hearing loss. It did not restore hearing (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02132130).

The 2024 reason why is unflattering and useful: in the adult mouse organ of Corti, ATOH1 alone does essentially nothing. Identity in a mature cell is held shut by more than one lock, and opening it took three factors at once — ATOH1 plus GFI1 plus POU4F3 — delivered to lineage-marked support cells whose neighbouring hair cells had first been killed off, because surviving hair cells actively suppress their neighbours' conversion (https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgae445). That produced hundreds of genuinely new, innervated hair cells per cochlea from cells that had never been sensory. It has not yet produced a mouse that hears better, and it asks a player to switch on, a few millimetres from the brainstem, the exact transcription factors that drive medulloblastoma.
Short Description: A deafened ear grows brand-new sound-sensing hair cells out of the flat support cells left behind after noise or drug damage — the repair birds perform by themselves and mammals lost. Adult quail regenerate so completely that hair-cell numbers return to within 5 percent of the original count. Forcing three hair-cell transcription factors together into adult mouse cochlear support cells yielded 479.9 ± 213.4 new lineage-traced hair cells per cochlea, against 2.8 ± 6.2 in controls and 46.0 ± 17.1 with ATOH1 alone. The one human attempt used that insufficient single-factor design: Novartis's CGF166 (NCT02132130) enrolled 22 patients and left treated ears 8.5 dB worse at week 52. The new cells are unfinished — PRESTIN, the motor protein that lets an outer hair cell amplify, appeared in only 45.6 ± 5.5% of them and not before six weeks — and this triad is a medulloblastoma transcriptional program switched on millimetres from the brainstem.
Mechanism: ATOH1 (atonal homolog 1) is a basic helix-loop-helix transcription factor that acts as the master regulator of hair-cell fate; GFI1 (growth factor independent 1) is a zinc-finger repressor that shuts down the supporting-cell and pro-apoptotic programs and stabilises the new identity; and POU4F3 (POU-domain class 4 transcription factor 3) drives hair-cell maturation and survival. In birds, supporting cells of the basilar papilla re-enter the cell cycle and transdifferentiate spontaneously. In mammals the ATOH1 locus is epigenetically locked and ATOH1 by itself is insufficient in the adult organ of Corti, so all three factors must be forced together in Lfng-lineage supporting cells to open the hair-cell gene network. Killing the endogenous hair cells first — using a diphtheria-toxin receptor knocked into the Pou4f3 locus — markedly raises conversion, which indicates that surviving hair cells laterally inhibit reprogramming through Notch signalling. The cells that result express MYO7A (myosin VIIA) and parvalbumin, acquire the outer-hair-cell motor protein PRESTIN, assemble ribbon-synapse proteins and rudimentary stereociliary bundles, and are contacted by nerve fibres (https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgae445).
Achievements (effect sizes): Adult Japanese quail whose basilar papilla had been damaged by acoustic trauma incorporated [3H]thymidine into hair-cell and supporting-cell nuclei within ten days, and an initial loss of hair cells recovered to within 5 percent of the original number of cells — the first demonstration that a vertebrate auditory epithelium regenerates after hatching (Ryals & Rubel 1988, https://doi.org/10.1126/science.3381101). In three-week-old mice carrying Lfng-CreERT2, a Rosa26-tdTomato lineage reporter and a Pou4f3 diphtheria-toxin receptor, tamoxifen-driven activation of Atoh1 together with Gfi1 and Pou4f3 after the endogenous hair cells had been killed produced 479.9 ± 213.4 tdTOMATO/MYO7A-double positive cells per cochlea (P = 0.0004 compared with control and P = 0.0034 compared with Atoh1 alone), against 2.8 ± 6.2 in control cochleas and 46.0 ± 17.1 with Atoh1 alone, a single-factor result that was not distinguishable from control (P = 0.9250) (https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgae445). Maturation lagged behind identity in the same animals: 45.6 ± 5.5% of regenerated hair cells co-labelled for MYO7A, PRESTIN and tdTomato at six weeks of age (N = 2) and PRESTIN was not detectable at all at five weeks, while 63.8% ± 3.7% (N = 2) of regenerated inner-compartment cells expressed parvalbumin compared with 8.8% ± 0.1% (N = 2) in the outer compartment (https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgae445).
Highest Evidence Tier: T6 (natural avian regeneration + adult-mouse three-factor reprogramming with lineage tracing + one completed human Phase 1/2 that failed on efficacy)
Translational Gaps: The cells produced by three-factor reprogramming are hair cell-like rather than finished hair cells: their stereociliary bundles are described as rudimentary and PRESTIN arrives late and in fewer than half of them, and no mammal has yet recovered an auditory threshold as a result of this manipulation. Nobody has solved how to deliver three coordinated transgenes to supporting cells along the whole length of the cochlear duct while sparing the spiral ganglion, whose neurons must survive for any regenerated cell to be heard. The protocol also depends on first destroying the surviving hair cells to lift Notch-mediated lateral inhibition, which is acceptable in a mouse that is already deaf but is a hard thing to ask of a patient with residual hearing. The single human trial tested the one-factor design that the mouse work has since shown to be inadequate, so the three-factor approach has never been given a clinical test at all.
Key References (DOIs): Ryals Science 1988 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.3381101 | McGovern PNAS Nexus 2024 https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgae445 | Izumikawa Nature Medicine 2005 https://doi.org/10.1038/nm1193 | Corwin Science 1988 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.3381100
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The literature disagrees about single-factor ATOH1, and the disagreement matters because a drug was built on one side of it. Izumikawa and colleagues reported that Atoh1 delivered alone improved hearing thresholds in deafened guinea pigs (Izumikawa 2005, https://doi.org/10.1038/nm1193), whereas the 2024 mouse study found that Atoh1 alone produced no increase in regenerated hair cells in the adult organ of Corti (46.0 ± 17.1 versus 2.8 ± 6.2 in controls, P = 0.9250) (https://doi.org/10.1093/pnasnexus/pgae445). Novartis's CGF166, an intralabyrinthine adenovector encoding human ATOH1, followed the single-factor design: 22 patients were enrolled and 19 completed, and the posted week-52 results show treated-ear pure-tone air-conduction thresholds moving in the wrong direction, +8.5 dB overall with cohort values of -4.2, +6.7, +26.3 and +5.0 dB (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT02132130). Those registry results have no journal publication, so they are recorded here from the registry rather than as a citable effect size, and the programme was not advanced. The avian half of the story is not contested: Ryals and Rubel (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.3381101) and Corwin and Cotanche (https://doi.org/10.1126/science.3381100) reported hair-cell regeneration in birds independently in the same year. One honest bookkeeping point: no ATOH1 entry exists for Coturnix japonica in UniProt, so the avian reference sequence given here is A0A0C6E596, the reviewed chicken (Gallus gallus) ortholog (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A0A0C6E596/entry). The quail supplies the natural regeneration phenotype; the reprogramming experiments were done in mice. No approved product exists and no company has a three-factor clinical candidate.

Narrative: Bdelloid rotifers survive radiation doses that would kill any vertebrate — partly thanks to a DNA repair enzyme they stole from bacteria. AvLigE is a prokaryotic DNA Ligase E acquired by horizontal gene transfer from bacteria into the rotifer Adineta vaga genome. When expressed in human cells, it significantly improves their radiation tolerance. This is evolution's most dramatic example of borrowing survival tools across the tree of life.
Short Description: Patches broken single strands in DNA after radiation damage, sealing breaks other repair enzymes leave open. Originally stolen from bacteria by a rotifer that survives radiation doses lethal to any vertebrate. Tested only in human cell lines in a dish, never in a living person. Because it's bacterial, it may not coordinate with the cell's own damage-signaling checkpoints, so its long-term behavior in a whole organism is untested.
Mechanism: AvLigE is a prokaryotic-type DNA ligase that catalyzes the final step of base excision repair and single-strand break repair. Its bacterial origin gives it distinct substrate preferences from eukaryotic ligases, providing complementary DNA repair capacity. In A. vaga, it is strongly upregulated after ionizing radiation exposure.
Achievements (effect sizes): Heterologous expression of AvLigE in human cell lines significantly improved radiation tolerance. Proteomic analysis confirmed it is a major DNA break repair contributor in irradiated rotifers. The gene was horizontally transferred from a prokaryote and is stably integrated in the rotifer genome.
Highest Evidence Tier: T4
Translational Gaps: Long-term effects of expressing a bacterial enzyme in human cells unknown. Integration with existing mammalian DNA repair pathways needs characterization. Potential interference with normal DNA damage signaling.
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: One of very few demonstrated cases of a horizontally transferred gene directly improving human cell function.

Narrative: Tardigrades can dry out completely, sit in a dusty drawer for years, and revive in a drop of water. The CAHS proteins are a big part of that trick. When water leaves the cell, CAHS D doesn't just stabilize molecules — it phase-separates into a glass-like mesh, freezing the cell's contents in place until rehydration. University of Wyoming researchers expressed CAHS D in human HEK293 cells in 2022; under osmotic shock, the protein formed the predicted reversible fibers inside human cells, slowed their metabolism, and modestly improved survival. But the story has gotten complicated fast. Piszkiewicz 2019 showed that plenty of unrelated proteins protect enzymes from drying just as well. Ramirez 2023 found that CAHS D doesn't actually hold onto water in the dry state, refuting a popular model. Non-gelling variants sometimes protect better than gelling ones. The protein is real and does something; nobody quite agrees on what.
Short Description: When water leaves the cell, this protein self-assembles into a glass-like mesh that locks enzymes in place until rehydration reverses it. Adding it to yeast boosted desiccation survival roughly 100-fold. Human HEK293 cells making it form the same fibers under osmotic shock and survive slightly better, but no mouse or long-term mammalian data exist. The catch: non-gelling versions protect enzymes better than the gel-forming original, so the mesh may not be the active ingredient.
Mechanism: Intrinsically disordered tardigrade-specific protein; reversible concentration/temperature-dependent gel/fibril networks; molecular shield against desiccation-induced unfolding.
Achievements (effect sizes): Boothby 2017 Mol Cell: yeast expressing CAHS D ~100× increased desiccation survival; E. coli also protected; RNAi of CAHS in tardigrades reduced post-desiccation survival. In vitro: protects LDH, lipoprotein lipase. Tanaka 2022 PLOS Biol (HEp-2, HEK293T): CAHS 1/3/8/12 form reversible filaments under hyperosmotic stress, stiffen cells (AFM), and modestly improve survival. Sanchez-Martinez 2024 Protein Sci (HEK293): CAHS D fibers slow metabolism and improve survival after 0.5 M sorbitol shock. Gel point ~8–20 g/L.
Highest Evidence Tier: T6 (HEK293, HEp-2, HeLa) + T3 (yeast/E. coli)
Translational Gaps: Stable long-term mammalian desiccation survival not shown; no mouse data; Esterly 2020 showed only safety in mice, not efficacy.
Key References (DOIs): Yamaguchi PLoS ONE 2012 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0044209 | Boothby Mol Cell 2017 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.molcel.2017.02.018 | Piszkiewicz Protein Sci 2019 https://doi.org/10.1002/pro.3604 | Tanaka PLoS Biol 2022 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pbio.3001780
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: CONTRADICTIONS: (1) Piszkiewicz 2019 — many unrelated globular/disordered proteins protect LDH similarly, CAHS specificity challenged. (2) Ramirez 2023 — CAHS D does NOT retain water in dry state, refutes water-replacement/retention model. (3) Gel-vs-protection mechanism contested: Sanchez-Martinez 2024 shows non-gelling variants protect citrate synthase BETTER than gelling WT. (4) Tanaka 2023 reply — GFP-only controls also form mesh in drying tardigrades; "filaments" may not be CAHS-specific in vivo. Non-physiological overexpression; modest mammalian-cell effects.

Narrative: A gecko can hang from a glass ceiling by a single toe because its foot-pads are covered in millions of microscopic hairs — setae — each tipped with even finer spatulas. The contact area gets so large that van der Waals forces alone are enough. No glue, no suction. The 2015 Gekko japonicus genome revealed a family of about 72 beta-keratin genes that make these setae, with bursts of duplication around 100 and 85 million years ago — matching the evolutionary origins of gecko adhesion. A single seta generates 20 to 40 micronewtons of force, and a whole foot can hold 40 times the animal's body weight. Synthetic gecko-inspired tapes, from polymer microfibers to carbon-nanotube arrays, already work reasonably well. But expressing gecko beta-keratins in mammalian cells to grow actual setae is a non-starter: the adhesion depends on a hierarchical anatomy — cells, pillars, hairs, spatulas — built by a developmental program, not on the protein sequence itself.
Short Description: Millions of hair-thin setae on gecko toes fan into spatula tips so small that van der Waals attraction alone locks them to glass, no glue, no suction. One seta pulls 20-40 micronewtons, letting a foot support 40 times the gecko's body weight. This only works in Gekko japonicus, whose genome shows 72 beta-keratin genes shaping the setae, and zero attempts to express them in other cells have grown a working spatula. The trick is architecture, not protein: skin must build hairs-on-hairs first.
Mechanism: Large multigene family (~71–72 CBPs); polymerize into ~3–4 nm β-sheet filaments in oberhautchen/beta-layer cells → setae → spatular tips (~200–500 nm); adhesion is PURELY van der Waals.
Achievements (effect sizes): Liu 2015 Nat Commun: G. japonicus genome (2.55 Gb); 72 CBP genes mapped to setae; phylogenetic expansions ~105–96 Mya and ~87–80 Mya. Alibardi IHC: Ge-cprp-9 in setae/spatular tips. Autumn 2000 Nature: single seta 20–40 μN; whole foot holds ~40× body weight. Autumn 2002 PNAS: van der Waals confirmed on polar + nonpolar surfaces; synthetic PDMS/polyester spatulae reproduce adhesion. ZERO heterologous CBP transfer producing functional setae. Gecko tape (Geim 2003 Nat Mater) + CNT gecko tapes (Qu 2008 Science) are SYNTHETIC — no protein, no gene.
Highest Evidence Tier: T1 (source organism) + T2 (protein biochem)
Translational Gaps: Gene transfer essentially a category error — adhesion requires hierarchical nanoarchitecture from developmental program, not compositional.
Key References (DOIs): Autumn Nature 2000 https://doi.org/10.1038/35015073 | Autumn PNAS 2002 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.192252799 | Liu Nat Commun 2015 https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms10033 | Geim Nat Mater 2003 https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat917
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Setae also contain lipids + α-keratins. CBP count disputed (26 vs 72 annotations) — underannotated repetitive family. Adhesion requires hierarchical nanoarchitecture from developmental program — not compositional.

Manipulation: loss-of-function (protein-truncating variants: premature stop, canonical splice-site disruption, or frameshift indels)
Narrative: This gene is in the library as a cautionary object as much as an enhancement. Cholesteryl ester transfer protein does one job in blood: it picks cholesteryl esters out of HDL particles and hands them to the apoB-containing lipoproteins, VLDL and LDL, taking triglycerides back in exchange. Block it and cholesterol stays in HDL. For twenty years that looked like the most obvious drug idea in cardiology - raise the good cholesterol, lower the bad one, with a single target. Pfizer took torcetrapib into ILLUMINATE, an outcome trial that enrolled 15,067 patients (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT00134264). It raised HDL cholesterol precisely as designed, and it increased all-cause mortality, so the trial was terminated (Barter 2007, https://doi.org/10.1056/NEJMoa0706628). Then evacetrapib and dalcetrapib were stopped for futility, and anacetrapib, which did reduce events modestly, was never commercialised, in part because the compound accumulated in fat tissue. Against that history, a group at the Broad Institute and Massachusetts General Hospital went back to human genetics with a specific question: forget the drugs, what happens to people who are simply born without this protein? They sequenced the gene's exons in 58,469 participants across twelve case-control studies and found carriers at a rate of about 1 in 975 - people with a premature stop, a disrupted splice site or a frameshift, which is as close to complete inhibition as nature provides. Those carriers had the lipid profile the drugs were aiming for and less coronary heart disease (Nomura 2017, https://doi.org/10.1161/CIRCRESAHA.117.311145). So the genetics say the target was right and the pills were wrong, and the field still does not agree on why - whether torcetrapib's off-target rise in blood pressure explains it, whether lifelong absence differs from late-life blockade, or whether the amount of cholesterol in HDL was never the causal quantity in the first place.
Short Description: Breaking the plasma shuttle that ferries cholesterol out of HDL particles and into the ones that build plaque leaves the cholesterol locked in HDL, where it does no harm. People born with a truncated version of that shuttle carry HDL cholesterol 22.6 mg/dL higher, LDL cholesterol 12.2 mg/dL lower, and 30% lower odds of coronary heart disease - the only entry in this library whose main effect is raising a lipid fraction rather than lowering one. No gene therapy or editor targets it; instead the drug version has a body count, because torcetrapib raised HDL exactly as designed and increased all-cause mortality, and evacetrapib and dalcetrapib both failed for futility. So this enhancement is a bet that a genotype present from conception behaves unlike the pill that phenocopies it, which is a bet the field keeps losing. The genetic effect sizes are also modest, with the LDL confidence interval reaching -0.98 mg/dL, almost nothing at all.
