Within this library it does not overlap EPAS1, which blunts the hypoxia-inducible factor response to thin air and concerns oxygen delivery; here oxygen is absent altogether and what changes is the end product of fermentation.

Narrative: You feel a feather brush against your skin because of PIEZO2 — a colossal ion channel shaped like a three-bladed propeller that converts mechanical force into electrical signals. Ardem Patapoutian won the 2021 Nobel Prize for discovering it. PIEZO2 sits in the tips of Merkel cell–neurite complexes in your skin and in proprioceptive neurons throughout your body. When tissue deforms, the channel opens and cations rush in, firing the sensory nerve. Humans with loss-of-function mutations in PIEZO2 lose the ability to feel light touch and proprioception — they cannot sense where their limbs are without looking. The protein is enormous: 2,752 amino acids forming a homotrimeric dome that curves the cell membrane and acts as its own force sensor. Woo and colleagues showed in 2014 that conditional knockout of Piezo2 in mouse Merkel cells completely abolished gentle-touch mechanosensitivity. The inverse experiment — overexpression to lower activation thresholds — has not been published, but the biophysics suggest that increasing PIEZO2 density could create tactile hypersensitivity comparable to the star-nosed mole. The main translational concern is that PIEZO2 gain-of-function mutations in humans cause distal arthrogryposis — excess mechanosensitivity can lock joints. A tissue-targeted overexpression strategy, restricted to skin Merkel cells, would be essential.
Short Description: This channel sits in skin and nerve endings, flexing open like a tiny propeller when the membrane stretches, letting ions rush in to fire a touch signal. Knocking it out in mice completely abolished gentle-touch sensing, so boosting it should lower that threshold. Overexpression has never been tested in any animal, only loss-of-function. The same gain-of-function effect in joint neurons causes Gordon syndrome, locking limbs before birth, so expression must stay out of muscle and joints.
Mechanism: PIEZO2 forms a homotrimeric propeller-shaped mechanically-activated cation channel (~2,800 kDa complex). The curved transmembrane dome acts as an area spring that flattens under membrane tension, gating the central pore. Ca²⁺ and Na⁺ influx depolarizes Merkel cells and sensory neurons, initiating touch and proprioceptive signaling.
Achievements (effect sizes): Woo 2014 Nature: conditional Piezo2 KO in mouse Merkel cells completely abolished gentle-touch mechanosensitivity. Delle Vedove 2016: human PIEZO2 LOF causes loss of proprioception and discriminative touch. Coste 2010 Science: identification of Piezo channels as first molecularly-defined mechanically-activated ion channels. 2021 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine (Patapoutian).
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (mouse conditional KO, multiple labs) + T7 (human genetic validation)
Translational Gaps: Gain-of-function overexpression not yet tested — only LOF phenotypes characterized. Need tissue-specific promoters restricting expression to Merkel cells to avoid systemic effects. No AAV/LNP delivery to cutaneous Merkel cells demonstrated.
Key References (DOIs): Coste Science 2010 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1193270 | Woo Nature 2014 https://doi.org/10.1038/nature13251 | Delle Vedove Am J Hum Genet 2016 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajhg.2016.09.019
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: CAUTION: Human gain-of-function mutations in PIEZO2 (e.g., E2727del) cause Gordon syndrome / distal arthrogryposis type 5 — excess mechanosensitivity causing prenatal joint contractures. Any enhancement strategy must restrict expression to cutaneous mechanoreceptors, not muscle or joint proprioceptors. The therapeutic window between enhanced touch and pathological mechanosensitivity is unknown.

Narrative: The shimmering iridescence of a pearl is no accident — it is engineered by a protein called Pif that orchestrates the formation of nacre, the nanostructured composite that makes mother-of-pearl 3,000 times more fracture-resistant than the pure mineral it's made from. Nacre consists of stacked aragonite crystal tablets uniformly oriented within a biopolymer scaffold, and Pif is the maestro conducting assembly. The akoya pearl oyster Pinctada fucata secretes Pif as a 1,007-amino-acid precursor that is cleaved into two functional domains: Pif97 (which anchors to the chitin framework) and Pif80 (which nucleates and orients aragonite crystal growth). Suzuki and colleagues proved Pif essential in 2009 by showing that RNAi knockdown disrupted nacre deposition. Clark and colleagues confirmed this with CRISPR-Cas9 in 2020. The biomimetic potential is extraordinary: nacre-like materials could reinforce bone, coat implants, or create self-healing armor. In human osteoblasts, Pif-directed mineralization could theoretically produce bone composite with nacre-like fracture resistance. The limitation is complexity: nacre formation requires not just Pif but also a chitin scaffold, controlled supersaturation, and the coordinated action of dozens of matrix proteins.
Short Description: A cleaved protein grabs a chitin scaffold with one half and glues aragonite crystals into it with the other, stacking them brick-by-brick into nacre. That composite is 3,000 times tougher than the raw mineral it's built from. So far it's only ever been done in the pearl oyster Pinctada fucata, where knocking the gene out stops nacre formation cold. Human bone uses hydroxyapatite, not aragonite, and needs 30+ other matrix proteins nacre relies on, so this protein alone builds nothing in people.
Mechanism: Pif precursor (1,007 aa) is cleaved into Pif97 (von Willebrand A domain binding the chitin framework) and Pif80 (acidic domain nucleating aragonite crystal growth). Together they direct layer-by-layer deposition of uniformly oriented aragonite tablets within an organic matrix, creating nacre's brick-and-mortar nanoarchitecture.
Achievements (effect sizes): Suzuki 2009 Science: Pif identified via CaCO₃-binding assay; RNAi knockdown disrupted nacre formation. Clark 2020 Biol Rev: CRISPR-Cas9 confirmed Pif's role. Nacre fracture toughness: 3,000× pure aragonite.
Highest Evidence Tier: T4 (pearl oyster in-vivo RNAi + CRISPR)
Translational Gaps: No vertebrate expression. Nacre formation requires ~30+ coordinated matrix proteins. Chitin scaffold absent in vertebrate bone. Aragonite is not the native CaCO₃ polymorph in vertebrate bone (which uses hydroxyapatite). Pif-directed mineralization in a hydroxyapatite system untested.
Key References (DOIs): Suzuki Science 2009 https://doi.org/10.1126/science.1173793 | Clark Biol Rev 2020 https://doi.org/10.1111/brv.12640 | Shi Mar Biotech 2012 https://doi.org/10.1007/s10126-012-9476-x
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Nacre formation is a system-level phenomenon. Pif is necessary but far from sufficient — over 30 matrix proteins have been identified. The aragonite/hydroxyapatite mismatch is a fundamental challenge: human bone uses a completely different mineral system. Primary application may be biomimetic materials engineering rather than genetic enhancement per se.

Manipulation: CAR T cell therapy (anti-uPAR scFv-CD28-CD3z); targets the gene product, not overexpression
Narrative:
Senescent cells are the body's retired workforce that refuses to leave the building. They stop dividing but do not die, and they leak inflammatory signals that degrade the tissue around them. Clearing them rejuvenates old mice. The problem has always been how: small-molecule senolytics kill by nudging stressed cells over an apoptotic threshold, which means dosing again and again as new senescent cells accumulate.

Corina Amor, working in Scott Lowe's laboratory at Memorial Sloan Kettering with the CAR T pioneer Michel Sadelain, asked a different question: what if senescent cells have a surface marker, and the immune system could be taught to read it? They found one — the urokinase plasminogen activator surface receptor, a protein tethered to the outside of the membrane that turns up on senescent cells whatever pushed them into senescence. Then they built the standard oncology tool against it: a second-generation chimeric antigen receptor, an antibody fragment fused to signalling domains, installed in T cells that thereafter kill anything wearing the marker.

The first paper (Amor 2020, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2403-9) showed this clears senescent cells from liver and reduces fibrosis. The follow-up (Amor 2024, https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-023-00560-5) asked what happens in an animal that is simply old. Twenty-month-old mice got one infusion. Their fasting glucose fell, they handled a sugar bolus better than untreated controls for over two hours, and most of them ran longer on a treadmill than they had before treatment — two and a half months after the single dose. Young mice showed no glucose effect, which is the right control: the therapy removes an age-specific burden rather than improving metabolism generally. Because CAR T cells expand and persist — the authors report persistence beyond 15 months — one dose buys surveillance instead of a pulse. An independent group has since done the same thing with a different receptor in aged monkeys. The unsolved part is not biology. It is that manufacturing an autologous cell product, and preceding it with lymphodepleting chemotherapy, is a great deal to ask of someone whose only complaint is being old.
Short Description: Arms your own T cells with a receptor that recognises a protein worn on the surface of worn-out senescent cells, so a single infusion hunts them out of liver, fat and pancreas and keeps patrolling afterwards. In 20-month-old mice one dose lowered fasting glucose, held plasma glucose down for more than two hours after a 2 g/kg glucose bolus, and improved treadmill endurance measured 2.5 months later; the same receptor covers 67–90% of the senescent burden in liver. No senolytic CAR T cell has ever entered a human trial — the clinical senolytics today are small molecules such as dasatinib plus quercetin and fisetin, which need repeated dosing. The protocol required cyclophosphamide preconditioning at 200 mg/kg, which is lymphodepleting chemotherapy in its own right, and the same receptor sits on activated immune cells and invasive tumour cells.
Mechanism: The urokinase plasminogen activator surface receptor (uPAR, encoded by PLAUR, 335 amino acids, anchored to the outer face of the plasma membrane by a glycosylphosphatidylinositol tail) is broadly upregulated on senescent cells regardless of what triggered the senescence, and Plaur is a component of the SenMayo senescence gene signature. The therapeutic agent is not the gene itself but a receptor aimed at it: a second-generation chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) built from an anti-uPAR single-chain variable fragment fused to a CD28 costimulatory domain and a CD3ζ signalling domain. Installed in T cells, it redirects them to lyse uPAR-positive cells through the perforin and granzyme pathway, with antigen-specific release of granzyme B and interferon gamma on engagement. The pharmacological distinction from small-molecule senolytics matters: because CAR T cells expand on antigen contact and persist afterwards, one infusion establishes durable immune surveillance of the senescent compartment rather than the transient kill-and-clear that repeated small-molecule dosing produces.
Achievements (effect sizes): Single-cell RNA sequencing of uPAR-positive and uPAR-negative cells sorted from 20-month-old mice established that the marker actually covers the population it needs to: uPAR-positive cells constituted 67–90% of the senescent cell burden in liver, 92–66% in adipose tissue and 76–63% in pancreas (Amor 2024, https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-023-00560-5). Treating aged mice with a single infusion of the anti-uPAR CAR, against both untransduced T cells and an irrelevant CAR as controls, significantly decreased fasting glucose, and after an intraperitoneal bolus of 2 g glucose per kg body weight the treated animals held significantly lower plasma glucose than controls for over 2 hours; most also showed improvements in exercise capacity 2.5 months after treatment compared with their own pretreatment levels (n = 7 untransduced, n = 8 irrelevant CAR, n = 8 anti-uPAR CAR for exercise testing), while young mice showed no such glucose effect (Amor 2024, https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-023-00560-5). The original demonstration was in liver: in an NRAS-G12V oncogene-induced senescence model, livers of CAR-treated mice had significantly reduced numbers of NRAS-positive (p<0.01) and senescence-associated beta-galactosidase-positive cells (p<0.001) versus controls, and in established liver fibrosis the treated livers showed fewer senescent cells and less fibrosis by senescence-associated beta-galactosidase and Sirius red staining (p<0.001) at 20 days, with under 2% of the CAR T cells displaying a triple-marker exhaustion phenotype at day 15 (Amor 2020, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2403-9).
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (mouse cell therapy across oncogene-induced, fibrotic, aged and high-fat-diet models in two papers from the same group, with independent confirmation of the approach using a different antigen; no human senolytic CAR trial)
Translational Gaps: No registered clinical trial of a senolytic CAR T cell exists. Searching the registry for uPAR CAR and for senolytic CAR T returns nothing; the only record that combines CAR engineering with senescence language is INT2104 from Kite/Gilead (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06539338), an in vivo lentiviral CD20 CAR for B-cell malignancies, which targets a different antigen in an oncology indication and is noted here only to document that the direction check was run and came back negative. Two practical barriers stand in the way. Manufacturing an autologous cell product for each patient is expensive and slow, and it has so far only been justified for fatal cancers rather than for ageing. The protocol also requires cyclophosphamide preconditioning, so a recipient takes lymphodepleting chemotherapy before receiving the cells. The authors additionally state that it remains undetermined which uPAR-positive populations actually drive the metabolic benefit, which means a safer, narrower antigen cannot yet be substituted for the broad one (Amor 2024, https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-023-00560-5).
Key References (DOIs): Amor Nature 2020 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2403-9 | Amor Nature Aging 2024 https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-023-00560-5 | Yang Science Translational Medicine 2023 https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.add1951
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: An independent group reached the same conclusion through a different antigen, which is the strongest available evidence that the approach and not the specific receptor is what works: NKG2D-targeting CAR T cells eliminated senescent cells in aged mice and in aged nonhuman primates without observed adverse effects (Yang 2023, https://doi.org/10.1126/scitranslmed.add1951). Durability is real — the 2024 paper reports CAR T cells persisting and expanding for over 15 months (https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-023-00560-5). Two cautions belong on the record. uPAR is not senescence-exclusive: the same receptor sits on activated immune cells and on invasive tumour cells, and the 2020 paper had to establish specifically that anti-uPAR CAR T cells do not attack normal tissue (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-020-2403-9). And senescence is itself tumour-suppressive and promotes wound healing, so clearing it systemically removes a genuine brake on premalignant expansion. The 2020 Nature paper carries an author correction (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-024-07197-3). Commercially, nothing is available: the closest clinical senolytics are small molecules — dasatinib combined with quercetin, and fisetin — which kill by a different mechanism and must be dosed repeatedly.

Narrative: Turritopsis dohrnii, a grape-sized jellyfish, can reverse its life cycle: a damaged adult collapses into a cyst and re-emerges as a juvenile polyp, resetting its biological age. It is the only animal known to do this reliably. In 2022, Carlos López-Otín's group sequenced its genome and identified a variant of POT1 — a human telomere-protection gene — predicted to release the brake on telomerase. When they put the G272N jellyfish mutation into the human POT1 protein, it bound telomeric DNA much less tightly in a test tube. That's the entire experimental result. No cell phenotype, no telomere-length measurement, no mammalian model. More worryingly, reduced POT1 binding in humans causes cancer — familial melanoma, leukemia, glioma. The paper has two formal Corrections and a published critique. Transdifferentiation is a whole-organism phenomenon; reducing it to a single shelterin variant is almost certainly too simple. The jellyfish is doing something astonishing, and nobody yet knows what.
Short Description: A grape-sized jellyfish can collapse into a cyst and regrow as a juvenile, resetting its own age. Scientists took its POT1 telomere gene, made one letter swap (G272N), and put it into human protein — in a test tube, it gripped its DNA anchor much more loosely. That's the whole result: no mammal, no cell, no telomere length ever tested. The same loosened grip in real humans is what causes familial melanoma and leukemia.
Mechanism: POT1 shelterin variant (G272N) predicted to reduce telomerase inhibition; SIRT3 mitoprotection; RTEL1 telomere helicase; GAR1 duplicated.
Achievements (effect sizes): Pascual-Torner 2022 PNAS: whole-genome T. dohrnii vs mortal T. rubra; identified expansions/variants. ONLY WET RESULT: introduced jellyfish-style G272N into recombinant human POT1, EMSA with 3×TTAGGG oligo → reduced ssDNA binding. No cell phenotype, no telomerase activity measured. Matsumoto/Miglietta 2025 bioRxiv: life-cycle-reversal transcriptome — SIRT3 peaks in cyst; RTEL1/HSP70/90 dynamic; POU/Sox/Klf/Myc detected. No functional tests. No gene editing in T. dohrnii; no mammalian transfer.
Highest Evidence Tier: T2–T3 for POT1 biochemistry on human-backbone protein; T1 for everything else
Translational Gaps: T. dohrnii POT1 in mammalian cells; telomere-length/cell phenotype; transdifferentiation never recapitulated in a mammal.
Key References (DOIs): Pascual-Torner PNAS 2022 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.2118763119
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: MAJOR CAVEAT: reduced POT1–ssDNA binding in humans = CANCER PREDISPOSITION. POT1 loss-of-function causes familial melanoma, CLL, glioma, pulmonary fibrosis (L259S, H266L). Pascual-Torner 2022 has TWO formal PNAS Corrections + a published critique by Miglietta 2023 PNAS. Annotation reliability for non-model organisms questioned. Binding ≠ function; 3×TTAGGG oligo is a minimal substrate.

Narrative: Deinococcus radiodurans survives 5,000 Gy — roughly a thousand times the lethal human dose. It does this by letting its genome shatter and then stitching it back together in hours, a feat coordinated by a single master-switch protein called PprI (or IrrE). When Chinese researchers gave human umbilical vein cells a shot of recombinant PprI before hitting them with 4 Gy of gamma rays, DNA damage markers dropped by about half. Mice treated with PprI before a 6 Gy whole-body dose had their 30-day mortality fall from 50% to 20%, with better blood counts and less organ damage. It's one of the cleanest demonstrations of bacterial radioresistance machinery working in a mammal. The caution is that this was essentially one paper from one lab, not independently replicated; the protein is bacterial (likely immunogenic); and the full Deinococcus resistance phenotype depends on manganese chemistry, not any single gene.
Short Description: This master-switch protein lets a bacterium called Conan shatter its genome under radiation, then stitch it back together in hours. Given to human cells before a 4 Gy dose, it cut DNA-damage markers by half; mice pretreated before 6 Gy saw 30-day death drop from 50% to 20%. It has never been tested in humans — only in mice and cultured HUVECs by one lab in China. Its bacterial origin makes it likely immunogenic, so it can't yet be dosed repeatedly as a protein.
Mechanism: PprI/IrrE: Mn-dependent zinc metalloprotease; cleaves repressor DdrO to derepress RecA, PprA, SSB; induces antioxidants (catalases). PprA: Deinococcus-specific DNA-end/nick-binding; stimulates ligase, interacts with gyrase/topo-IB.
Achievements (effect sizes): Gao 2003 DNA Repair: IrrE in E. coli → ~1.6× γ-IR survival at 50/100 Gy; upregulated RecA, KatG. Pan 2009 PLoS ONE: IrrE → salt/oxidative/thermal tolerance in E. coli and Brassica. Shi 2016 Sci Rep: HUVECs (human cells) pretreated with 4 μg/mL Pichia-produced PprI + 4 Gy γ: D0 1.58→1.66 Gy, Dq 0.99→1.54 (larger shoulder); ~50% γH2AX foci reduction at 1–8 h; reduced apoptosis; ↑RAD51. SAME PAPER, BALB/c mice, 6 Gy TBI + PprI 100 μg/kg IP: 30-day mortality 50%→20% (5/10 → 2/10); improved WBC/platelets; reduced lung fibrosis, hepatic/renal damage. Zhang 2017: plasmid-pprI in-vivo electroporation in mice pre-6 Gy also reduced mortality +30%.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (PprI mouse, single lab) + T6 (HUVECs)
Translational Gaps: Independent replication; long-term safety; humanized/PEGylated protein or mRNA delivery.
Key References (DOIs): Gao DNA Repair 2003 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.dnarep.2003.08.012 | Pan PLoS ONE 2009 https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0004422 | Shi Sci Rep 2016 https://doi.org/10.1038/srep29220 | Zhang 2017 (oncotarget) https://doi.org/10.18632/oncotarget.13893
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Deinococcus-specific DdrO substrate is ABSENT in mammals — mechanism in human cells is indirect (antioxidants + RAD51). E. coli gain only 1.6× (vs ~1000× Deinococcus native resistance). Daly's work shows Deinococcus resistance is primarily Mn-peptide proteome protection, not PprI/PprA alone. Bolus protein dosing not translation-ready; bacterial-protein immunogenicity. PprA has no robust standalone mammalian in-vivo evidence.

Narrative:
Proteorhodopsin was found in the ocean before it was found in an organism. A shotgun-sequencing survey of surface seawater turned up a rhodopsin gene on a bacterial DNA fragment catalogued as EBAC31A08, belonging to the SAR86 clade — a group of gammaproteobacteria nobody had ever grown in culture. The gene existed as a database entry before anyone could hold the cell that carried it, and what it encodes is a light-driven proton pump that lets an ordinary heterotroph run part of its energy budget on sunlight without performing photosynthesis at all.

What the protein does is mechanically simple and biologically radical. A seven-helix opsin holds a molecule of vitamin A aldehyde, all-trans-retinal, buried in the middle of the membrane. A green photon bends the retinal, the protein flexes through a conformational cycle, and one proton is carried from the inside of the cell to the outside. Do that continuously and you have a proton gradient — the same electrochemical currency the respiratory chain builds, and one that can be spent directly on adenosine triphosphate synthesis or on spinning a flagellum.

The experiment that proved the point, done in the Liphardt laboratory at Berkeley, is memorable for its brutality. Escherichia coli carrying the gene were poisoned with sodium azide, which shuts down the respiratory chain, and then put in sunlight. Cells with the pump and its retinal cofactor kept swimming and kept forming colonies; cells with the pump but no retinal did worse than cells with nothing at all, because an opsin without its chromophore is a piece of membrane hardware that does nothing (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0611035104). That control is the honest heart of this card. In the dark, or on a vitamin-A-poor diet, the enhancement is not neutral — it is a liability. And because the pump absorbs green light, which is among the worst wavelengths for getting through tissue, a body-scale version would need a light source inside it.
Short Description: A light-driven proton pump sits in the cell membrane and keeps the proton gradient charged from sunlight alone, so the cell keeps moving and stays alive when its respiration has been poisoned or the oxygen has run out. Absorbing a single green photon bends the vitamin-A cofactor inside the protein and shoves one proton across the membrane, building the same voltage a mitochondrion would. In sunlight, 11% of Escherichia coli carrying the pump plus retinal survived 30 minutes in 30 mM sodium azide against 1% of cells with retinal alone, and green light restored a poisoned cell's flagellum to the rotation speed of an unpoisoned one. The gene was pulled out of seawater DNA before anyone cultured the bacterium, and the only animal work targets related archaeal pumps to mitochondria in flies and worms, never to a plasma membrane. It is dead weight in the dark and useless without dietary vitamin A: cells expressing the opsin with no retinal did worse than cells with no opsin at all.
Mechanism: Proteorhodopsin is a 249-amino-acid, 27.3 kDa seven-transmembrane opsin. It binds all-trans-retinal, the aldehyde form of vitamin A, through a Schiff base to a lysine residue on its seventh helix, which buries the chromophore in the middle of the lipid bilayer. Absorption of a green photon isomerises that retinal to its 13-cis form, and the strained chromophore drives a cycle of conformational changes in the protein during which one proton is translocated vectorially across the membrane. The gradient this builds — the proton-motive force — is the identical currency produced by the respiratory electron transport chain, which is why it can power the flagellar motor and adenosine triphosphate (ATP) synthase directly, with no electron transport, no oxygen and no quinone pool. The variant on this card is the green-light-absorbing form; a blue-absorbing relative from deeper water differs at a small number of residues that retune its absorption maximum, so the family as a whole reads as a depth gauge for the sunlit ocean.
Achievements (effect sizes): The decisive experiment poisoned respiration and asked whether light could replace it. Escherichia coli were exposed to 30 mM sodium azide for 30 minutes in sunlight under four conditions — with and without proteorhodopsin, with and without exogenous all-trans-retinal — and then plated for colony counts: “the cells lacking retinal were most sensitive to azide; no colonies were recovered after plating the azide exposed cells. The cells lacking PR but having retinal were slightly more azide resistant; 1% of cells survived. The cells with both PR and retinal were significantly more azide resistant than in all three other conditions (11% of cells survived; P < 0.005, Mann-Whitney U test)” (Walter 2007, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0611035104). A single-cell version of the same logic measured proton-motive force directly, by watching one tethered bacterium's flagellum turn across an azide titration from 0 to 110 mM: “the pmf dropped to 50% of its original value at an azide concentration of 55 mM... When the cells were illuminated with intense green light, their rotation rate was restored to the speed of cells with an unimpaired respiratory system”, and the same work estimated the pump's Michaelis-Menten constant at 10^3 photons per second/nm2 (Walter 2007, https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0611035104).
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (heterologous gain-of-function in bacteria with single-cell biophysics and survival endpoints; related mitochondrially targeted proton pumps validated in Drosophila and C. elegans by independent laboratories)
Translational Gaps: In an animal this class of pump has only ever been used inside mitochondria, never at the plasma membrane, and never as proteorhodopsin itself. Imai and colleagues targeted delta-rhodopsin from the archaeon Haloterrigena turkmenica to Drosophila mitochondria and recovered mitochondrial membrane potential and motor behaviour in a CHCHD2 model of Parkinson's disease (https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-019-0674-1). Berry and colleagues targeted a light-driven proton pump to the mitochondria of Caenorhabditis elegans and extended lifespan (https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-022-00340-7). Both experiments depend on feeding the animal retinal, because neither the fly nor the worm can synthesise it, and neither used the marine proteorhodopsin of this card. No mammalian in vivo work exists at all. Nobody has measured whether a human cell tolerates a light-gated proton leak in its plasma membrane, and nobody has solved the optical problem: green light penetrates tissue poorly, so a body-scale version would need either an implanted illuminator or a red-shifted pump that has not been built.
Key References (DOIs): Walter Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 2007 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0611035104 | Imai Communications Biology 2019 https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-019-0674-1 | Berry Nature Aging 2022 https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-022-00340-7
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: This gene is a good exhibit for how sequencing changed biology. It was found by environmental shotgun sequencing of seawater rather than by culturing an organism, so the sequence was in a database before anyone had the bacterium; the host is recorded simply as gamma-proteobacterium EBAC31A08 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/Q9F7P4). Structures exist at three levels and can be shown side by side: a solution nuclear magnetic resonance structure of the green-absorbing pump (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/2L6X), a cryo-electron microscopy structure of the same protein (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/7B03), and crystal structures of the blue-absorbing variant that occupies a different depth in the water column (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/4KLY and https://www.rcsb.org/structure/4KNF), which lets the display show spectral tuning against ocean depth. There are no clinical trials and no commercial product for proteorhodopsin. The one clearly negative result in the record deserves to stay on the wall rather than be quietly dropped: cells expressing the opsin without retinal were the worst of the four conditions tested, not merely equivalent to untreated cells (https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.0611035104). Finally, the mitochondrially targeted animal work uses different rhodopsins from different archaea and should not be read as validation of this particular gene (https://doi.org/10.1038/s42003-019-0674-1, https://doi.org/10.1038/s43587-022-00340-7).

Narrative: Bats and dolphins both hear well into the ultrasonic range — frequencies far above anything a human or mouse can detect — and they evolved this ability independently. The molecular centerpiece is prestin, a motor protein in cochlear hair cells that physically contracts in response to voltage, amplifying faint sounds. Echolocating bats and dolphins carry the exact same amino-acid substitutions in prestin, a textbook example of convergent molecular evolution, and those substitutions change the protein's electrical properties when measured in human HEK293 cells. This is where the press ran ahead of the data. Yalin Li's lab showed in 2022 that prestin-knockout mice still hear above 40 kHz — prestin amplifies loudness but doesn't determine frequency range. Tian 2021 found that prestin's electrical parameters don't actually correlate with how high an animal can hear. Nobody has yet put bat prestin into a mouse and extended its hearing. The convergent evolution is beautiful; the functional story is shakier than it first looked.
Short Description: Inside the ear, this motor protein squeezes and stretches with each sound wave, amplifying faint vibrations before hair cells detect them. Dolphin prestin shifts its voltage midpoint to −61 mV, a change measured only in human cells in a dish. No one has placed it into a mouse to extend hearing range. The catch: prestin-knockout mice still hear above 40 kHz fine, so this motor boosts loudness, not ultrasonic range.
Mechanism: Outer hair cell voltage-driven piezoelectric motor protein; non-linear capacitance (NLC) parameters Qmax/Clin, V½, 1/α.
Achievements (effect sizes): Liu 2014 MBE: 7 species' prestins in HEK293, whole-cell NLC. 1/α significantly increased in all echolocators (N7T attributed); V½ depolarized in dolphin and Stoliczka's trident bat (I384T attributed). Bavi/Santos-Sacchi 2021–2023 dolphin prestin HEK293: V½ −61 mV, 1/α 37 mV; visible electromotility. No knock-in mouse carrying bat/dolphin prestin has been published. Prestin-KO mice: ~50 dB threshold elevation high-freq; Cheatham 2012 V499G/Y501H KI: ~34% residual charge, defective high-freq amplification.
Highest Evidence Tier: T3 (HEK293 NLC, multiple labs)
Translational Gaps: No bat/dolphin prestin-KI mouse gain-of-function; mouse hearing range not extended.
Key References (DOIs): Liu Curr Biol 2010 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2009.11.058 | Liu MBE 2014 https://doi.org/10.1093/molbev/msu157
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: CONTRADICTIONS: (1) Li 2022 Neurosci Bull — prestin-KO mice RETAIN >40 kHz hearing — prestin amplifies amplitude, is NOT the ultrasonic selectivity determinant. (2) Tian 2021 Front Cell Dev Biol — NLC parameters DO NOT correlate with species Fmax — direct challenge to the "prestin drives ultrasonic hearing" narrative. (3) Shen 2012 — Pteronotus CF bat lacks rhinolophid adaptive signature — convergence incomplete. HEK293 ≠ cochlear micromechanics; Qmax depends on expression; site-direction on common backbone ≠ full-length.

Manipulation: overexpression of a stabilised decuple variant (PtUGT1stable)
Narrative:
Indigo is the oldest blue humans have, and it has always been a chemically awkward one. The pigment is insoluble, so to get it into cloth you must first destroy it: a traditional vat reduces indigo to its soluble leuco form with harsh reducing agents in strongly alkaline water, soaks the yarn, then lets air oxidise the dye back to blue inside the fibre. Denim is dyed this way at a scale of tens of thousands of tonnes a year, and the reducing agents and alkali are the reason blue jeans have an environmental reputation.

The dyer's knotweed of Japan solves the same problem from the other direction. Rather than making indigo and then having to un-make it, the plant makes indoxyl, the reactive monomer, and immediately caps it with a sugar. The product, indican, is colourless, water-soluble and stable, and it stays that way until the cap comes off. Break the leaf, or add a beta-glucosidase, or simply shine light on it, and free indoxyl is released, dimerises, oxidises in air and becomes indigo. This is a pigment stored as a loaded spring, and it is the basis of fermentation indigo dyeing as practised for centuries.

The enzyme doing the capping, PtUGT1, is a perfectly good plant enzyme and a poor industrial one: at the indoxyl concentrations bulk production needs, it inactivates. A protein-engineering campaign fixed exactly that, combining ten stabilising substitutions into a single variant that melts 13.1 degrees Celsius higher without losing wild-type activity, and then ran the whole process through both a techno-economic model and a life-cycle assessment (Bidart 2024, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45749-3). The result is honest in a way such papers often are not. Dyeing with indican is dramatically cleaner than the conventional vat, but producing indican is very slightly dirtier than producing indigo, and the whole case rests on a yield figure sitting one percentage point from break-even. For an enhancement library the interest is the chemistry itself: colour held in reserve, colourless until something opens it.
Short Description: Your tissue stockpiles a colourless sugar-capped precursor that turns deep indigo blue the moment it is cut open and hit by light or an enzyme, a dye that develops on contact with air rather than being painted on. The enzyme caps reactive indoxyl with a glucose to keep it inert, and an engineered version carrying ten stabilising substitutions gained 13.1 degrees Celsius of melting temperature while converting 65% of a 100 millimolar indoxyl feed. Applied to denim rather than to bodies, this route cuts the environmental impact of blue dyeing by 73% when the colour is released by light and 92% when released enzymatically. It has only ever been run as an in vitro enzymatic process and a lab-scale dyeing protocol, never in a plant or animal host. The saving is also not free upstream: making indican costs 1.2% more in monetised environmental terms than conventional indigo, 21.0 against 20.7 US dollars per kilogram, and marine eutrophication actually gets worse.
Mechanism: PtUGT1 is a uridine-diphosphate-dependent glucosyltransferase (UGT) that transfers glucose onto indoxyl to make indican, that is indoxyl-beta-glucoside, a stable, colourless, water-soluble storage form of the pigment precursor. Removing the glucose again, either enzymatically with a beta-glucosidase or photolytically under light, releases free indoxyl, which spontaneously dimerises and oxidises in air to indigo, the pigment itself. The plant uses this as a precursor-storage strategy, keeping the reactive indoxyl capped and inert until it is needed. Industrially the same chemistry replaces the conventional indigo vat, which needs harsh reducing agents and strongly alkaline conditions to solubilise pre-formed indigo, because with indican the dye is generated inside the yarn under mild conditions instead. The wild-type enzyme suffers severe substrate inactivation at the indoxyl titres bulk production requires, and it was this inactivation, rather than catalytic rate, that the stabilising engineering was designed to overcome.
Achievements (effect sizes): The engineering result is a stability gain with no activity penalty. Mutations with a favourable effect on melting temperature were combined into a decatuple variant designated PtUGT1stable, which showed a Delta Tm of +13.1 degrees C (+13.8 kcal/mol) while retaining wildtype activity (Bidart 2024, https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45749-3). That stability translated into process performance: the variant achieved 65% conversion of 100 mM indoxyl in an inexpensive phosphate-citrate buffer, against a techno-economic viability threshold the authors had set at 60% conversion of at least 100 mM indoxyl with uridine-diphosphate-glucose recycling and replacement of the HEPES buffer by a pH stat (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45749-3). A cradle-to-factory-gate life-cycle assessment then compared indican dyeing against the conventional indigo vat and found that photolytic, light-driven release would reduce the environmental impact of blue denim dyeing with 73%, compared to a 92% reduction offered by enzymatic dyeing, and that indican dyeing has the potential to reduce human lifetime loss, biodiversity loss and financial loss from resource depletion to 9, 10 and 6% respectively of conventional-dyeing losses (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45749-3). The same assessment declines to overclaim: producing indican rather than conventional indigo at 65% yield carries a 1.2% increase, which can be monetarized to 21.0 USD/kg versus 20.7 USD/kg, and the authors note that raising the yield from 65 to 66% would make the two equal, while the dyeing step itself costs 1.5-fold conventional, or 0.08-0.14 USD per pair of jeans at scale (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45749-3).
Highest Evidence Tier: T4 (engineered enzyme characterised in vitro, demonstrated dyeing process, plus techno-economic and life-cycle assessment; not yet at industrial scale)
Translational Gaps: Everything demonstrated here happened in a test tube and a dye bath. The work established an in vitro enzymatic process and a laboratory-scale dyeing protocol, and nobody has expressed the engineered enzyme in a plant or an animal host or run the process at industrial scale, so the card's body framing is an extrapolation from plant chemistry rather than a reported phenotype. The techno-economic case also depends on recycling uridine-diphosphate-glucose efficiently at scale, and the authors model that recycling rather than demonstrating it in an industrial reactor. The life-cycle numbers carry a similar caveat: they were computed against the current European electricity grid mix, and the authors state that a fully renewable energy input would change them substantially. Because the margin is thin, small process losses matter more than they would in a mature route.
Key References (DOIs): Bidart Nature Communications 2024 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45749-3
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Two closely related UniProt accessions cover this enzyme family in Persicaria tinctoria and it is easy to cite the wrong one. A0A2Z5UHQ8 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A0A2Z5UHQ8) is annotated as indican synthase 2 at 497 amino acids, while A0A2R2JFJ4 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/A0A2R2JFJ4) is 478 amino acids and is the accession cross-referenced by Protein Data Bank entry 5NLM (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/5NLM), a 2.14 angstrom structure titled as a complex between a UDP-glucosyltransferase from Polygonum tinctorium capable of glucosylating indoxyl; Polygonum tinctorium is the older synonym for Persicaria tinctoria, so the two species names in the literature refer to one plant. Both accessions have AlphaFold models. On availability, the engineered enzyme is not a product: plant-derived indican and indigo from Persicaria tinctoria and Isatis tinctoria are sold today as natural dyes, but the PtUGT1stable route remains pre-commercial and has no clinical dimension at all (https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-024-45749-3). Two caveats on the environmental claim deserve recording rather than smoothing over. Marine eutrophication is reported as getting worse under the indican route, and human toxicity and mineral resource scarcity rise because of the sodium phosphate manufactured for the dyeing buffer, so the 73% and 92% headline reductions describe the dyeing step and not the whole supply chain. The authors also report a viability floor: below 53% conversion the process ceases to be economically viable, which sits uncomfortably close to the 65% achieved. This entry also fills the plant kingdom, previously absent from the database entirely.

Narrative: The sleeping chironomid Polypedilum vanderplanki is the only insect that can dry out completely and come back to life — its larvae survive total water loss in African rock pools for years. A major part of its trick is a family of 27 Late Embryogenesis Abundant (LEA) proteins, intrinsically disordered molecules that form protective glass-like matrices as water leaves the cell. The 2014 genome project by Gusev and colleagues found these genes massively expanded and clustered on Chromosome 4 — an evolutionary hotspot for desiccation innovations. LEA proteins from anhydrobiotic organisms have been expressed in mammalian cells: independent groups showed LEA fusions localize to cytoplasm and mitochondria in HepG2 hepatoma cells and sheep fibroblasts, protecting against acute desiccation damage. Gusev's team confirmed PvLEA localization in mammalian and insect (Sf9) cells, though GFP-fusion localization varied between constructs and cell lines. The mechanism is distinct from tardigrade CAHS proteins: while CAHS D forms reversible gel-like fibers, LEA proteins act through vitrification — forming an amorphous solid that physically immobilizes biomolecules. The limitation is real: LEA glass formation requires very low water content, and human cells don't naturally dehydrate that far. Still, for biopreservation of cells, tissues, or organs, LEA engineering is one of the most-studied routes.
Short Description: As cells lose water, this protein turns glass-like, locking membranes and enzymes in place instead of letting them shred apart. Its source, a chironomid larva, carries 27 copies of the gene and survives years bone-dry in African rock pools. Tested only in isolated human liver and sheep skin cells, with no living mammal ever dried and revived. It needs near-total water loss, which human tissue never reaches, so its future is drying organs for storage.
Mechanism: Intrinsically disordered proteins that undergo vitrification (glass-state transition) at low water activity; physically immobilize and shield biomolecules and membranes during desiccation. Reinforced by trehalose-based glassy matrix. 27 paralogues in P. vanderplanki clustered on Chromosome 4.
Achievements (effect sizes): Gusev 2014 Nat Commun: genome revealed 27 PvLEA genes massively upregulated during anhydrobiosis. Li 2012: Artemia LEA group 3 protected human HepG2 cells from desiccation, maintained membrane integrity. Marunde 2013: AfrLEA3m protected sheep fibroblasts during air-drying. Kondratyeva 2022: PvLEA-GFP fusions localized to cytoplasm/mitochondria in mammalian and Sf9 cells. In vitro: LEA proteins protect LDH, citrate synthase, and liposomes from dehydration-induced damage.
Highest Evidence Tier: T4 (mammalian cell expression, localization confirmed) + T3 (cross-species functional protection)
Translational Gaps: No stable mammalian transgenic; no in-vivo drying survival demonstrated; vitrification requires near-complete dehydration beyond physiological range; GFP-fusion localization inconsistent between constructs.
Key References (DOIs): Gusev Nat Commun 2014 https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms5784 | Kondratyeva Biology 2022 https://doi.org/10.3390/biology11040487 | Yoshida NAR Genomics 2022 https://doi.org/10.1093/nargab/lqac029 | Li J Exp Biol 2012 https://doi.org/10.1242/jeb.064063
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: LEA vitrification requires very low water content — human cells do not naturally reach this state. GFP-fusion artifacts: localization differed between N-terminal and C-terminal fusions (Kondratyeva 2022). LEA proteins are highly redundant — 27 paralogues raises the question of which are essential vs. vestigial. Overlap with CAHS D: both protect against desiccation but through different physical mechanisms (glass vs. gel). Biopreservation is the realistic use case, not whole-organism desiccation tolerance.

Narrative: Bdelloid rotifers (Adineta vaga) survive complete desiccation for decades — losing virtually all body water and reviving when rehydrated. PvLiL (LEA-like protein from bdelloid rotifers) is a Late Embryogenesis Abundant protein that forms a protective glass-like matrix around cellular components during drying, preventing protein aggregation and membrane fusion. This molecular vitrification shield preserves life without water.
Short Description: When cells dry out, this protein coats membranes and proteins in a glass-like mesh, holding them in place so they can't clump or tear apart. Bdelloid rotifers that make it survive complete desiccation for 9+ years, then rehydrate with everything intact. So far this trick has only been shown working in transplanted mammalian cells in a dish, never in a living human. It works only alongside other protective proteins, since this one alone likely can't cover the full desiccation-survival job.
Mechanism: PvLiL is an intrinsically disordered protein that transitions to an alpha-helical glass-like state upon dehydration. It coats membranes and proteins, preventing deleterious interactions during water loss. Upon rehydration, it dissolves back to its disordered state, releasing protected components intact.
Achievements (effect sizes): Bdelloid rotifers survive complete desiccation for 9+ years. Heterologous LEA protein expression protects mammalian cells from desiccation damage. LEA proteins from related organisms stabilize enzymes and liposomes during drying.
Highest Evidence Tier: T3
Translational Gaps: Bdelloid rotifer-specific LEA proteins are less characterized than Polypedilum vanderplanki PvLEA. Full desiccation tolerance likely requires multiple protective proteins working in concert.
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Complements existing PvLEA (sleeping chironomid) and CAHS D (tardigrade) desiccation genes. Bdelloid rotifers represent a distinct evolutionary solution.

Narrative: Proteins accumulate damage over time — one of the most common lesions is the spontaneous conversion of aspartate and asparagine residues into isoaspartate, which kinks the backbone and kills function. Every organism has at least one enzyme to fix this: protein L-isoaspartate methyltransferase (PIMT). Humans have one copy. The sleeping chironomid has fourteen. Gusev's 2014 genome project revealed this dramatic gene expansion, and later work showed PIMTs are among the most overexpressed genes during both desiccation and ionizing radiation exposure — the molecular repair crew works overtime whenever proteins get beaten up. Deviatiiarov 2020 characterized the family in detail: only PIMT1 and PIMT2 retain classical enzymatic activity; the others appear to have acquired novel functions through subfunctionalization. Shaikhutdinov 2023 found that the closely related P. pembai (which is also desiccation-tolerant) independently amplified PIMTs to 6 copies with radical structural changes, suggesting strong positive selection on protein repair. The human orthologue PCMT1 is well studied — PCMT1-knockout mice die within 42 days of seizures and brain damage. Overexpression of PCMT1 in Drosophila extends lifespan under heat stress. The chironomid's solution is simple brute force: more copies, more repair, more survival.
Short Description: Old proteins kink when aspartate warps into isoaspartate, jamming the backbone; PIMT bends it back. This chironomid carries 14 copies of that repair gene versus one in humans, flooding them out during desiccation and radiation. Mice lacking their single copy die by day 42 in seizures, while flies given extra human copies live 30% longer under heat stress. No mammal has tested more than one copy, so whether extra doses help neurons or overload them is untested.
Mechanism: SAM-dependent methyltransferase that converts L-isoaspartate back to L-aspartate via a methyl ester intermediate. 14 paralogous copies in P. vanderplanki (vs. 1 in most insects/mammals). Subfunctionalized: only PIMT1/PIMT2 retain canonical enzymatic activity; others may have acquired novel repair or regulatory roles.
Achievements (effect sizes): Gusev 2014: 14 PIMT paralogues identified, among most upregulated genes during anhydrobiosis. Deviatiiarov 2020: expression profiling across 5 clusters; only PIMT1/2 enzymatically active. Shaikhutdinov 2023: P. pembai independently amplified PIMTs to 6 copies with radical structural changes under positive selection. Kim 2002: PCMT1-knockout mice die by day 42 (seizures). Chavous 2001: Drosophila PCMT overexpression extends lifespan ~30% under heat stress.
Highest Evidence Tier: T4 (P. vanderplanki expression/functional data) + T3 (Drosophila/mouse orthologue studies)
Translational Gaps: No mammalian PIMT overexpression study; unclear which of the 14 paralogues are most protective; subfunctionalized copies may not all transfer useful activity; human PCMT1 is essential but whether more is better is unknown.
Key References (DOIs): Gusev Nat Commun 2014 https://doi.org/10.1038/ncomms5784 | Deviatiiarov Insects 2020 https://doi.org/10.3390/insects11090634 | Shaikhutdinov GBE 2023 https://doi.org/10.1093/gbe/evad169 | Chavous PNAS 2001 https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.141221698
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Amplification strategy assumes more copies = more repair, but subfunctionalization means many paralogues have diverged in function. PCMT1-null mice die young — the enzyme is essential, but the dose-response curve for overexpression is unstudied in mammals. P. pembai shows a completely different PIMT architecture, suggesting there is no single optimal solution even among chironomids. No direct cross-species expression in mammalian cells yet.

Narrative: Hibernating ground squirrels cool their bodies to near freezing for months — yet their brains emerge unscathed. When a human brain drops below 33°C during cardiac arrest, neurons die from failed synapse regeneration. The difference comes down to RBM3, a cold-shock RNA-binding protein that orchestrates synapse rebuilding during rewarming. Peretti and colleagues published a landmark study in Nature in 2015 showing that RBM3 is the key mediator of cooling-induced neuroprotection. In both prion-infected and Alzheimer's (5XFAD) mouse models, the capacity to regenerate synapses after cooling declined in parallel with loss of RBM3 induction. When they overexpressed RBM3 via lentivirus in the hippocampus — without any cooling — the results were dramatic: restored synapse reassembly, prevented behavioral deficits, prevented neuronal loss, and significantly prolonged survival in both disease models. Follow-up work mapped the signaling pathway: TrkB-PLCγ1-pCREB activates RBM3 transcription, and RTN3 is the downstream effector promoting synapse formation. The human RBM3 gene exists and is functional — it's just not strongly cold-induced in adult humans the way it is in hibernators. Overexpression could bring the benefits of therapeutic hypothermia without the hypothermia.
Short Description: Rebuilds synapses after cold or disease damage, the way a squirrel's brain repairs itself waking from hibernation. Lentiviral overexpression in mouse hippocampus, no cooling needed, extended survival in both prion and Alzheimer's (5XFAD) models. All findings come from one lab, the MRC Prion Unit, with no independent replication yet. It's disease rescue in mice, not human enhancement, and RBM3 stabilizes mRNA broadly, risking effects beyond the synapse.
Mechanism: RBM3 is a 157-aa RNA-binding protein with an N-terminal RNA recognition motif (RRM) and glycine-rich C-terminal domain. Upregulated during hypothermia via TrkB-PLCγ1-pCREB signaling. Promotes synapse reassembly through downstream effector RTN3, facilitating neurite outgrowth and synapse formation. Also broadly stabilizes mRNAs at low temperature.
Achievements (effect sizes): Peretti 2015 Nature: lentiviral RBM3 overexpression in mouse hippocampus restored synapse reassembly, prevented behavioral deficits and neuronal loss, significantly extended survival in both prion (RML) and Alzheimer's (5XFAD) models — without cooling. Peretti 2021: TrkB agonism induces RBM3 without cooling. Bastide 2017: RTN3 identified as downstream neuroprotective effector.
Highest Evidence Tier: T5 (mouse in-vivo overexpression with survival endpoint in two disease models)
Translational Gaps: Single laboratory (MRC Prion Unit) — not independently replicated. Effect demonstrated in disease rescue, not healthy brain enhancement. AAV delivery to human hippocampus is invasive. Long-term effects of constitutive overexpression unknown. RBM3 affects global mRNA stability — transcriptome-wide side effects possible.
Key References (DOIs): Peretti Nature 2015 https://doi.org/10.1038/nature14142 | Peretti Life Sci Alliance 2021 https://doi.org/10.26508/lsa.202000884 | Bastide Curr Biol 2017 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cub.2017.01.047
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Published in Nature with robust survival data, but all key experiments from one laboratory (Giovanna Bhatt group, MRC Prion Unit). Independent replication critical. Effect is disease rescue, not enhancement above normal — the 'hibernation in a bottle' framing is attractive but unvalidated. RBM3 is a global RNA chaperone; constitutive overexpression may have unintended transcriptome effects. TrkB agonism (pharmacological RBM3 induction without cooling) may be more attractive than direct gene delivery.

Narrative: Cuttlefish and octopuses change color in milliseconds by telling reflectin proteins inside special skin cells to reorganize. Reflectin is weirdly rich in methionine and arginine and self-assembles into stacked layers that act as tunable mirrors. In 2020, Alon Gorodetsky's group at UC Irvine stably expressed squid reflectin in human HEK293T cells; the protein condensed into intracellular nanoparticles, and when researchers changed the salt concentration outside the cells, the reflectin condensates reversibly swelled and shrank, modulating how the cells scattered light. Media outlets called it 'invisible human cells,' which overstates a genuinely cool result: what changed was the cells' refractive index by a few percent, not their transparency to the naked eye. Cephalopod skin also needs chromatophore organs — pigmented sacs under fine neural control — that simply don't exist in mammals. Reflectin, by itself, is a promising biomaterial with medical-imaging potential; adaptive camouflage for humans is not in the cards.
Short Description: Skin cells pack this protein into dense nanoparticles that swell or shrink, bending light like a built-in tunable mirror. In 2020, HEK293T cells carrying squid reflectin shifted refractive index from 1.4 toward the cytoplasm's 1.33–1.38 just by changing outside salt levels. That's the ceiling so far: only cultured human cells in a dish, no mouse or zebrafish. Real cuttlefish camouflage also needs chromatophore organs — nerve-controlled pigment sacs mammals don't have.
Mechanism: Reflectins (~20–60% Met/Tyr/Arg) self-assemble into membrane-bound lamellar Bragg stacks; phosphorylation-controlled hydration tunes reflectance.
Achievements (effect sizes): Kramer 2007 Nat Mater: recombinant squid reflectin in E. coli forms films/gratings/fibers; ammonia/acid triggers visible spectrum shifts. Chatterjee 2020 Nat Commun: stable HEK293T lines expressing D. opalescens reflectin A1 — condensed into intracellular nanoparticles; quantitative phase microscopy showed leucophore-like contrast; NaCl osmotic challenge REVERSIBLY modulated light scattering (refractive index n≈1.4 vs cytoplasm 1.33–1.38); tens of percent transmittance changes across visible/NIR. Gorodetsky lab reflectin-coated films: tens of percent reversible IR reflectance with stretch — MATERIALS, not tissue.
Highest Evidence Tier: T6 (HEK293T in vitro) + T3 (E. coli films)
Translational Gaps: No in-vivo mammal; no tissue-level camouflage; requires innervated chromatophores in native animal.
Key References (DOIs): Kramer Nat Mater 2007 https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat1930 | Chatterjee Nat Commun 2020 https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-019-08891-x
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Press framing ("invisible human cells") OVERSTATES result: effect is refractive-index modulation only, not perceptible transparency. Structural biology of reflectin contested (IDP, no crystal structure). No mouse/zebrafish demonstration.

Narrative: A flea jumps 150 times its own body length because its legs contain resilin — nature's most efficient rubber. This elastomeric protein stores and returns 92–97% of mechanical energy, outperforming any synthetic rubber. Insects use it for high-frequency wing hinges, jumping pads, and sound-producing tymbals. Resilin was first described by Torkel Weis-Fogh in 1960, and the gene was identified in Drosophila melanogaster as CG15920. The protein is largely intrinsically disordered (~94%), gaining its extraordinary elasticity from entropic recoil — stretched resilin spontaneously recoils because the disordered chains seek maximum entropy, like a rubber band. Cross-linking occurs in vivo via dityrosine bridges catalyzed by peroxidase. Qin and colleagues showed in 2011 that recombinant resilin from Drosophila exon 1, expressed in E. coli and photo-cross-linked, formed solid biomaterials with ~90% resilience and high extensibility. Resilin-like polypeptides are actively pursued for tissue engineering: cardiovascular grafts, cartilage repair, and vocal fold reconstruction. In human tissue, resilin expression in tendons, ligaments, or vocal cords could confer insect-level elastic energy storage and fatigue resistance — imagine tendons that never degrade from repetitive strain.
Short Description: Stretchy chains in insect legs and wings snap back almost perfectly after being pulled, storing energy like a rubber band instead of losing it as heat. Locust wing hinges made of it return 97% of that energy per bounce. It has only been tested as lab-made biomaterial in dishes, never grown inside any vertebrate tendon or ligament. Making it work in you needs an enzyme to weld the chains together at a precise dose, since uncontrolled cross-linking would damage surrounding tissue.
Mechanism: Resilin is an intrinsically disordered protein that achieves near-perfect elasticity through entropic recoil. Predominantly glycine/proline-rich chains lack stable secondary structure and behave as freely-jointed polymer chains. Cross-linking via dityrosine bonds (catalyzed by peroxidase) creates a covalent elastomeric network with 92–97% energy return efficiency.
Achievements (effect sizes): Qin 2011: recombinant Drosophila resilin exon 1 formed biomaterial with ~90% resilience after photo-cross-linking. Qin 2009: full-length resilin expressed, chitin-binding domain characterized, cross-linked materials showed excellent elastomeric properties. Weis-Fogh 1960: measured 97% resilience in locust wing hinge.
Highest Evidence Tier: T3 (recombinant expression in E. coli, biomaterial characterization) + T4 (insect in-vivo)
Translational Gaps: No mammalian tissue expression. Dityrosine cross-linking requires controlled enzyme activity — uncontrolled cross-linking could damage tissue. Integration into existing extracellular matrix unknown. Mechanical loading differs between insect cuticle and mammalian tendon.
Key References (DOIs): Qin Biomaterials 2011 https://doi.org/10.1016/j.biomaterials.2011.06.010 | Qin Biomacromolecules 2009 https://doi.org/10.1021/bm900735g | van Eldijk Top Curr Chem 2012 https://doi.org/10.1007/128_2011_205
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: No study has expressed resilin in any vertebrate tissue. The 620-aa Drosophila pro-resilin includes a signal peptide (17 aa) and a chitin-binding domain (exon 2) not relevant for human expression — typically only exon 1 (elastic repeats) is used. The path from E. coli expression to in-vivo tendon enhancement is long. Resilin-like polypeptides (RLPs) are among the most promising protein biomaterials but remain pre-clinical.

Narrative:
Reverse gyrase is the closest thing molecular biology has to a diagnostic signature. It is the only protein found exclusively and universally in hyperthermophiles — the organisms that live above 80 C in hydrothermal vents and hot springs — and its presence in a genome is used as the definitive marker for that lifestyle. Structurally it is a fusion of two familiar parts: a topoisomerase IA domain welded to a helicase-like ATPase. Functionally it does something no other enzyme does, introducing positive supercoils into closed circular DNA, tightening the helix rather than relaxing it as bacterial gyrase does.

For years the supercoiling was assumed to be the point, on the reasonable theory that overwinding a helix would resist thermal melting. The more interesting answer turned out to be mechanical. Reverse gyrase recognises nicked DNA, recruits a cooperative coat of protein onto the lesion, and holds the strands in register so a single-strand nick cannot propagate into a double-strand break; it also keeps denatured regions from tangling and helps them re-anneal correctly. This chaperone-like protection needs neither ATP hydrolysis nor any supercoiling activity, which means the enzyme has a second job entirely separable from the one it was named for — it is a splint, not a winch (https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkh683).

The literature then produced a beautiful apparent contradiction. One paper is titled to say reverse gyrase is not a prerequisite for hyperthermophilic life; another says it is essential for microbial growth at 95 C. Both are right. Knock the gene out of Thermococcus kodakaraensis and the organism still grows at 90 C, merely more slowly as the temperature rises (https://doi.org/10.1128/jb.186.14.4829-4833.2004). Delete it from Pyrococcus furiosus, which prefers 100 C, and growth at 95 C and above stops outright (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00792-017-0929-z). Together the two papers bracket a threshold near 90 C, above which the splint becomes non-negotiable. That threshold is also this card's hardest limitation, because a human being does not live anywhere near it.
Short Description: Your DNA stops snapping when you overheat: a molecular splint clamps onto a nicked double helix and holds the strands together at temperatures that would otherwise break the genome apart. It recognises the nick, coats the lesion with a cooperative protein layer, and physically prevents a single-strand cut from opening into a double-strand break — no repair chemistry and no ATP hydrolysis required. Purified enzyme cut the rate of double-strand breakage roughly eight-fold at 90 C, and deleting it from Pyrococcus furiosus makes the archaeon unable to grow at 95 C or 100 C. This has only ever been done in archaea and in a test tube; nobody has expressed reverse gyrase in a eukaryote of any kind. Below the threshold it buys nothing while still costing something: a Thermococcus knockout grows fine at 90 C, and at 37 C the enzyme would burn ATP and impose positive supercoiling that runs opposite to the negative supercoiling human topoisomerases maintain for transcription and replication.
Mechanism: Reverse gyrase is a topoisomerase IA domain fused to a helicase-like adenosine triphosphatase (ATPase) domain, 1,214 amino acids and about 140 kDa in Pyrococcus furiosus. Its namesake activity is the introduction of POSITIVE supercoils into closed circular DNA, the opposite of what bacterial gyrase does. The thermoprotective function, however, is separable from supercoiling. The enzyme recognises nicked DNA, recruits a cooperative coat of protein molecules onto the lesion, and then acts as a physical splint that stops a single-strand nick from propagating into a double-strand break; at the same time it prevents denatured stretches of DNA from aggregating inappropriately and promotes their correct re-annealing. This chaperone-like protection requires no ATP hydrolysis and is independent of the positive-supercoiling activity, so the two functions can be uncoupled experimentally. Nothing in this description is repair: no base is excised, no phosphodiester bond is remade to restore a lost nucleotide. The enzyme prevents damage from getting worse rather than reversing damage already done.
Achievements (effect sizes): The mechanistic result is a straight in vitro measurement. Purified reverse gyrase incubated with DNA at 90 C “reduces the rate of double-stranded DNA breakage approximately 8-fold at 90 degrees C” relative to a protein-free control, and the authors report that this activity does not require ATP hydrolysis and is independent of the enzyme's positive-supercoiling activity (Kampmann 2004, https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkh683). Genetics in living archaea then bracketed when the protection actually matters. Deleting the gene from Pyrococcus furiosus, an organism whose optimal growth temperature is 100 C, showed that “the gene is required for growth at 95 degrees C, as well as at 100 degrees C”, leading the authors to conclude that a temperature threshold above 90 C exists above which reverse gyrase is absolutely necessary (Lipscomb 2017, https://doi.org/10.1007/s00792-017-0929-z). The boundary condition comes from a different genus: in Thermococcus kodakaraensis KOD1, whose optimum is 85 C, “the disruption of the reverse gyrase gene did not lead to a lethal phenotype at 90 degrees C”, although positive-supercoiling activity present in the host strain was absent from the disruptant and growth retardation became more striking as temperature rose (Atomi 2004, https://doi.org/10.1128/jb.186.14.4829-4833.2004). A third laboratory, a third organism and a third method extended the phenotype to chemical DNA damage: knocking down topR1 by endogenous type III-B CRISPR-Cas messenger-RNA interference in the thermoacidophilic crenarchaeon Sulfolobus islandicus and challenging the cells with the alkylating agent methyl methanesulfonate showed that “the survival rate of pKD-topR1/E233S1 was about four times lower than pSeSD1/E233S1 during 1.3 and 2 mM MMS treatment and about 90 times lower during 2.6 mM MMS treatment” (Han 2017, https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms18071340).
Highest Evidence Tier: T3 (in vitro biochemistry plus loss-of-function genetics in three archaeal species from independent laboratories; no heterologous gain-of-function in any eukaryote)
Translational Gaps: Every quantified result in this record is either purified-enzyme biochemistry or loss of function in an archaeon. Nobody has expressed reverse gyrase in a mesophilic eukaryote and then measured thermotolerance, so the gain-of-function direction this card frames has never been tested in the direction it is framed. Delivery is a second obstacle with a hard number attached: the protein is 1,214 amino acids in Pyrococcus furiosus and 1,711 in Thermococcus kodakarensis, which puts its coding sequence near the practical ceiling for packaging into a single adeno-associated viral vector. There is also a plausible mechanistic conflict that has not been experimentally examined: human topoisomerases maintain negative supercoiling to support transcription and replication, and an enzyme that adds positive supercoils would be working against them. Whether a human cell tolerates that has not been measured in any system.
Key References (DOIs): Kampmann Nucleic Acids Research 2004 https://doi.org/10.1093/nar/gkh683 | Lipscomb Extremophiles 2017 https://doi.org/10.1007/s00792-017-0929-z | Atomi Journal of Bacteriology 2004 https://doi.org/10.1128/jb.186.14.4829-4833.2004 | Han International Journal of Molecular Sciences 2017 https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms18071340
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: The apparent contradiction in the titles is real and worth putting on the wall rather than smoothing over. One paper is titled to say reverse gyrase is not a prerequisite for hyperthermophilic life (https://doi.org/10.1128/jb.186.14.4829-4833.2004) and another that it is essential for microbial growth at 95 C (https://doi.org/10.1007/s00792-017-0929-z). Both conclusions hold, because they were reached in different organisms at different temperatures, and read together they define a threshold near 90 C: disrupting the gene in Thermococcus kodakaraensis is survivable at 90 C, whereas the Pyrococcus furiosus gene is required at 95 C and 100 C. Structural depiction requires care. The deposited structures 4DDT (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/4DDT), 3P4X (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/3P4X) and 3OIY (https://www.rcsb.org/structure/3OIY) are all of the Thermotoga maritima homologue, UniProt O51934 (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/O51934); no experimental structure of the Pyrococcus enzyme (https://www.uniprot.org/uniprotkb/P95479) exists, so any image of it is an AlphaFold prediction and should be labelled as one. There are no clinical trials and no commercial product. The enzyme's practical uses today are as a research reagent and as the definitive phylogenetic marker for hyperthermophily. Supporting loss-of-function evidence now spans three archaeal genera and three independent methods — gene disruption in Thermococcus, deletion in Pyrococcus, and CRISPR interference in Sulfolobus (https://doi.org/10.3390/ijms18071340) — which is unusually broad for a gene with no eukaryotic data at all.

Narrative: The silver spinyfin (Diretmus argenteus) has the most complex visual system of any vertebrate — 38 rod opsin genes where most fish have one. By expressing multiple tuned rhodopsins in its retina, each absorbing a slightly different wavelength, the spinyfin can distinguish colors in the near-total darkness of the deep ocean using only rod photoreceptors. This breaks the textbook rule that rod cells cannot do color vision.
Short Description: Rod cells normally sense only dim light, not color, but this deep-sea fish split its rods into over a dozen types, each tuned to a different blue wavelength. Its most extreme variant, RH1-1, absorbs light at just 444 nm, the bluest rod pigment ever found in a vertebrate. Gene therapy already restores one rhodopsin gene in humans (Luxturna); this fish runs 14 of 38 duplicated copies at once. No lab has tried a multi-opsin version in mammals, so it stays deep-sea biology only.
Mechanism: Through tandem duplication of the RH1 (rhodopsin) gene, the spinyfin expresses 14+ rod opsins tuned to wavelengths from 444-519 nm. Key spectral tuning sites (including positions 83, 122, 261, 292) carry substitutions that shift absorption peaks. Co-expression of differently tuned opsins in separate rod populations enables wavelength discrimination without cone cells.
Achievements (effect sizes): The most blue-shifted rod photopigment known (RH1-1, ~444 nm) was characterized from spinyfin. 14 of 38 RH1 genes are expressed in adult retina. Three independent deep-sea fish lineages evolved expanded RH1 repertoires convergently.
Highest Evidence Tier: T3
Translational Gaps: Rod opsin engineering for human therapy is speculative. Retinal gene therapy for single genes is feasible (Luxturna), but multi-opsin systems are far more complex. Basic science value is primary.
Key References (DOIs): https://doi.org/10.1126/science.aav4632
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Breaks the vertebrate 'one rod opsin' rule. Three independent evolutionary origins of multi-RH1 systems in deep-sea fish.

Narrative: Deer antlers are the fastest-growing bone in the animal kingdom — up to 2 cm per day. S100A10 (annexin A2 ligand) is a calcium-binding protein highly enriched in the antler growth zone that accelerates osteoblast proliferation and bone mineralization. Stanford researchers showed that antler progenitor cells can stimulate bone repair in mice, with S100A10 as a key driver of this extraordinary growth rate.
Short Description: On osteoblast surfaces it partners with annexin A2 to boost calcium flux, pushing bone cells to multiply and mineralize fast. Deer antler bone grows over 20 kg a year at up to 2 cm a day, driven by this protein in the growth zone. So far it's only worked in mice, where implanted antler progenitor cells sped up fracture healing. Rapid bone growth carries an untested cancer risk in humans, and the antler's other growth factors this gene alone may not replace.
Mechanism: S100A10 forms a complex with annexin A2 on osteoblast surfaces, enhancing calcium signaling and plasminogen activation. In antler periosteum, it is dramatically upregulated during the rapid growth phase, promoting progenitor cell proliferation, extracellular matrix deposition, and accelerated mineralization through enhanced calcium flux.
Achievements (effect sizes): Antler-derived progenitor cells implanted in mice accelerated bone fracture healing. S100A10 is among the most differentially expressed genes in antler growth zones. Deer antlers regenerate 20+ kg of bone annually with zero cancer risk.
Highest Evidence Tier: T4
Translational Gaps: Antler growth involves a complex niche of progenitor cells, growth factors, and vascular networks. S100A10 alone may be insufficient. Cancer risk from stimulating rapid bone growth in humans needs evaluation.
Key References (DOIs): https://doi.org/10.1126/science.add0488
Notes (limitations, contradictions, cave: Paired with UHRF1 (epigenetic regulator) from same Stanford deer antler study.

Narrative:
Syntrichia caninervis is a desert moss and probably the toughest multicellular organism in this library. Li and colleagues reported in 2024 that it recovers photosynthetic and physiological activity within seconds of rehydration after losing more than 98% of its cellular water, regenerates after three or five years at -80 degrees C and after 15 or 30 days in liquid nitrogen, has an estimated gamma-radiation LD50/1h of about 5,000 Gy in the dry state against about 2,000 Gy when hydrated, and survives simulated Mars conditions with its capacity to regenerate intact (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xinn.2024.100657). None of that is attributed to this gene, and the honest version of the story keeps the organism and the enzyme apart.

What the gene does is narrower and much better measured. Every one of those insults - drying, salinity, ionising radiation - peroxidises membrane lipids, and peroxidised lipids break down into reactive aldehydes such as malondialdehyde and 4-hydroxynonenal that then attack proteins and DNA. ScALDH21 is a single-copy aldehyde dehydrogenase from a family found only in mosses, and it oxidises those aldehydes to their corresponding acids. A group at the Xinjiang Institute of Ecology and Geography in Urumqi cloned it, put it into tobacco (https://doi.org/10.1016/j.plaphy.2015.07.001), then into upland cotton, and took the cotton all the way to a field trial under water withholding, where the transgenic plants outyielded controls without losing fibre quality (https://doi.org/10.1007/s11032-015-0422-2).

This is the least theatrical kind of stress resistance and possibly the most useful. It is not a shield and not a radical scavenger: it is a mop for the damage products that get past both, which is why it works on drought, salt and oxidative stress with the same chemistry. In a human body the same logic would apply to any tissue that peroxidises its own membranes under load - and so would the complication that the aldehyde being mopped up is also a messenger.
Short Description: Drought, salt and radiation all burn membrane lipids, and the burning leaves reactive aldehydes behind that crosslink proteins and DNA; this enzyme oxidises them into harmless acids first. Cotton engineered with it accumulated roughly 11.8-304% more proline than non-transgenic cotton under drought, carried less lipid-peroxidation aldehyde, and in the field grew taller, set larger bolls and yielded more fibre with no loss of fibre quality. It comes from a desert moss that regains photosynthesis seconds after rewetting from the loss of over 98% of its water and survives simulated Mars conditions - whole-organism feats, not this gene's. It has only ever been expressed in plants, tobacco and cotton, with field trials in China and no commercial cultivar. The cost is that it consumes the signal along with the poison: 4-hydroxynonenal is how a cell detects oxidative attack, and the same chemistry in a human belongs to ALDH2, the liver enzyme that clears acetaldehyde after alcohol.
Mechanism: ScALDH21 is an aldehyde dehydrogenase of 483 amino acids and roughly 53 kDa that depends on the oxidised nicotinamide cofactor NAD(P)+, and it belongs to aldehyde dehydrogenase family 21 - a family unique to mosses and represented there by a single-copy gene. When drought, high salinity or ionising radiation peroxidise membrane lipids, the damaged lipids release reactive electrophilic aldehydes: malondialdehyde (MDA), 4-hydroxynonenal and related lipid-derived carbonyls, all of which form covalent adducts with proteins and with DNA. The enzyme oxidises these aldehydes to their corresponding carboxylic acids, removing the electrophile and regenerating the reduced cofactor NAD(P)H. That places it downstream of the antioxidant enzymes rather than alongside them: it is chemical detoxification of a damage product, not radical scavenging and not physical shielding, so it clears the damaging species that survive after superoxide dismutases, catalases and peroxidases have already acted.
